**Surah 16 (al-Nahl)**

*Meccan, except for three verses at its end. It is also called Surat al-Ni'am (the Surah of Blessings). It has 128 verses. [It was revealed after Surat al-Kahf.]*

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.**

They used to seek to hasten what they had been promised of the Hour's coming or of the punishment descending upon them on the Day of Badr, mocking and denying the promise. So it was said to them: ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾, which is in the position of what has arrived and is occurring, even though it was still awaited because its occurrence was near. ﴿So do not seek to hasten it.﴾

It is reported that when ﴿The Hour has drawn near﴾ was revealed, the disbelievers said among themselves: "This man claims that the Resurrection has drawn near. So let us refrain from some of what we do, until we see what will happen." When it was delayed, they said: "We see nothing." Then ﴿Their reckoning has drawn near for people﴾ was revealed, so they became fearful and awaited its nearness. When the days lengthened, they said: "O Muhammad, we see nothing of what you threaten us with." Then ﴿The command of Allah has come﴾ was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sprang up and the people raised their heads, so ﴿so do not seek to hasten it﴾ was revealed, and they were reassured.

It was also recited as *tasta'jilūhu* with the *ta'* and with the *yā'* (i.e., *tasta'jilūhu* read with a second-person and with a third-person verb form).

﴿Glorified and exalted is He above what they associate (with Him).﴾ He, Mighty and Majestic, declares Himself free from having any partner, and from their gods being partners with Him. Or (it means) above their associating (others with Him). Here *mā* (ما) may be a relative pronoun (*mawṣūla*) or a verbal-noun particle (*maṣdariyya*), that is, a particle which, with the verb following it, forms a verbal noun.

If it is asked: "How does this connect with their seeking to hasten (the punishment)?" The answer is: because their seeking to hasten it was mockery and denial, and that is a form of *shirk* (associating partners with Allah).

It was also recited as *tushrikūna* with the *ta'* and with the *yā'* (i.e., the verb read as *yushrikūna* or *tushrikūna*).

The passage is read as yunazzilu (with both light and heavy forms of the verb). It is also read as tanazzalu al-malaikatu (the angels descend), meaning they descend with the Spirit (al-ruh) by His command, with that which gives life to hearts dead through ignorance from His revelation, or with that which in religion stands in the place of the spirit in the body. "An anzirū" is a substitution (badal) for "al-ruh": that is, He sends them down with the instruction "warn." Its underlying construction is: "bi-annahu anzirū," meaning: "that the matter is, I say to you: warn." Alternatively, "an" may be explanatory (mufassirah), because the sending down of the angels with revelation carries the meaning of speech.

The meaning of "anzirū annahu lā ilāha illā anā" is: know (a‘lamū) that the matter is so, from "nadhirtu bi-kadha" when one has come to know it. The sense is: He says to them, "Inform the people of my word: there is no god but Me, so fear Me" (fa-ittaqūni).

Then He indicated His oneness and that there is no god but Him by what was mentioned: things that none other than He can do, namely the creation of the heavens and the earth, the creation of man and what sustains him, and the creation of livestock, which he needs for food, riding, hauling his loads and all his other needs, and the creation of what they do not know of the various kinds of His creatures. Someone like Him is too exalted to have anything associated with Him.

It is also recited as "tushrikūn" (you associate), with both the ta' and the ya'. ﴿Then, behold, he is an open adversary﴾. This has two meanings. The first: then, behold, he is one who speaks clearly, who argues in defense of himself, who confronts his opponents and makes the proof manifest, after having been a drop of semen, inert matter with no sensation and no movement, as a sign of His power. The second: then, behold, he is an adversary to his Lord, one who denies his Creator, saying: "Who will give life to bones when they are decayed?" This describes man as extreme in insolence and ignorance, and persistent in ingratitude for blessings.

It is said that it was revealed concerning Ubayy ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi, when he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with a decayed bone and said:

"O Muhammad, do you think God will give life to this after it has decayed?" [[It will come in the commentary on Surah Yasin.]]

**al-An'am** (the livestock) are the eight kinds of pairs (*al-azwaj al-thamaniyah*), and the term applies most often to camels. It is in the accusative because of an implied verb that the explicit verb interprets, as in His saying ﴿and the moon—We have measured it﴾ (36:39). It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with *al-insan* (man), meaning: He created man and the livestock. Then He said, ﴿He created them for you﴾, meaning: He did not create them except for you and for your benefits, O human race.

**al-Difʾ** (warmth) is the name of what one is warmed by, just as **al-Milʾ** (filling) is the name of what one fills with. It is the warmth obtained from clothing made of wool, fur, or hair. It has also been read as *duff*, with the hamza dropped and its vowel placed on the *fa'*. ﴿And benefits﴾ refers to their offspring, their milk, and other things.

If you ask: the fronting of the adverbial phrase in His saying ﴿from them you eat﴾ indicates restriction, yet people also eat from other animals. I say: eating from them is the basic kind, the one on which people rely for their livelihoods. As for eating from other animals, such as chickens, ducks, and game of land and sea, it is like something not counted as significant and is treated as a matter of enjoyment and luxury.

[[Mahmud said: "If you say, why was the prepositional phrase fronted? He answered that eating from them is the basic (origin)..." etc.? Ahmad said: The basis of this explanation is that fronting the complement of a verb makes it restricted to that complement, as if he had said, "You only eat from them."]]

It is also possible that your sustenance comes from them, because you plough with cattle, so the grain and fruits you eat come from them, and you earn a living by hiring out camels and selling their young, their milk, and their hides.

God has bestowed favour upon you by the beauty they add, just as He has bestowed favour by the benefit derived from them, for this is among the aims of the owners of livestock; indeed it is among its greatest aims. When the herdsmen bring them back in the evening (yurawwihuna) and send them out to pasture in the morning (yusarrihuna), they adorn the courtyards with their bringing back and sending out, and the bleating (al-thughaa') and lowing (al-rughaa') echo within them [[On his words "and the bleating and lowing echo within them": al-thughaa' is the sound of sheep and goats and what resembles them; al-rughaa' is the sound of animals with hooves (dhawat al-khuff), as stated in al-Sihah.]]. They delight their people, gladden their owners, make them honoured in the eyes of those who behold them, and win them standing and esteem among people. A similar idea is found in His words: ﴿And [He created] them for you to ride and as adornment﴾, ﴿It covers your nakedness and is a source of finery﴾. If you ask: why is bringing back mentioned before sending out? I answer: because beauty is more evident in the bringing back, when they come home with full bellies and heavy udders, and then retire to their pens, presenting themselves to their people.

And Ikrimah recited: ﴿Ḥīnan turīḥūna wa-ḥīna tasraḥūn﴾ (with the verb in the form tarīḥūna and ḥīna tasraḥūn), taking ḥīna as a descriptive (ṣifah) for the time. The meaning is: you bring them back at it and send them out at it, as in His words Exalted be He: ﴿a day when no parent will avail anything﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 7:

It is read as bi-shiqq al-anfus (بشق الأنفس), with the shin both kasra'd and fatha'd. It is said that they are two dialects with the same meaning, meaning hardship, but there is a difference between them:

The fatha'd form is a verbal noun (masdar) of shaqqa al-amr 'alayhi shaqqan (شق الأمر عليه شقا), "the matter was hard for him," and its underlying sense goes back to the shaqq (شق), which is a cleft or split.

As for the kasra'd form, shiqq (شق), it means a half, as if one loses half his strength through the exertion he undergoes. If you say: what is the meaning of His words, ﴿you would not have been able to reach it﴾? It is as if they spent a period of time bearing hardships in reaching it, until the camels carried their loads. I say:

Its meaning is: "and [the camels] carry your loads to a land you would not have reached, by hypothetical estimation, had the camels not been created, except through the exertion of your own selves"; not that they in reality could not have reached it. If you say: how does His words, ﴿you would not have been able to reach it﴾, correspond to His words, ﴿and they carry your loads﴾? Why was it not said: "you would not have been able to carry them to it"? [Mahmud said: "If you say, how does His words 'you would not have been able to reach it' correspond to His words 'and they carry your loads'...?" Ahmad said:

It is possible that the intended meaning is: "and they carry your loads to a land which you would not have reached with them except through the exertion of your selves," and he dispensed with mentioning the reaching in place of mentioning carrying them, because it is customary that a traveler cannot dispense with loads he takes along. The first meaning is higher, and God knows best.] I say: its correspondence lies in that its meaning is: "and they carry your loads to a distant land which you know you would not reach by yourselves except through effort and hardship, let alone that you could carry your loads on your backs." It is also permissible that the meaning be: "you would not have reached it with them except through the exertion of your selves." It is said that "your loads" means "your bodies." It is reported from Ikrimah that the land is Makkah. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾, since He showed mercy to you by creating these beasts of burden and facilitating these benefits.

And the horses, the mules, and the donkeys (﴿وَالْخَيْلَ وَالْبِغالَ وَالْحَمِيرَ﴾) are a conjunction (ʿatf) with the cattle (al-anʿam), meaning: He created these for riding and adornment. He used this to argue for the prohibition of eating their flesh, since He gave the reason for their creation as riding and adornment and did not mention eating, after mentioning it in the case of the cattle.

If you ask: why is ﴿وَزِينَةً﴾ in the accusative? I answer: because it is a maf'ul lahu (object of purpose, i.e. an accusative of reason), and it is conjoined to the position (maḥall) of ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوهَا﴾.

If you ask: why did the conjoined and the conjoined-to not come in the same pattern? [Mahmud said: "If you say, why did the conjoined and the conjoined-to not come in one pattern...?"] Ahmad said: He means that it would have been permissible for it to be in the accusative stripped of the particle of causation (lam al-taʿlil), because it is the act of the agent of the first verb; and what confirms this is that riding is joined with the lam, because it is the act of those addressed. Whenever the agent is not the same, the lam must be attached. In this answer, however, there is room for examination, for an objector can say: it was possible for both to come with the lam, so they would come in one pattern. There is no harm in this, for the question stands, and the ready answer to it is: the principal, intended purpose in these kinds of animals is riding, while adornment by them is a subsidiary matter that is not intended in the way riding is intended. So the important intended purpose was joined with the lam which conveys causation, to draw attention to the fact that it is the more important of the two aims and the stronger of the two causes; and adornment was stripped of it, to draw attention to its being subordinate to riding or falling short of it. And God knows best.

I say: because riding is the act of those addressed, whereas adornment is the act of the one who adorns, and that is the Creator.

It is also read: ﴿لِتَرْكَبُوهَا زِينَةً﴾ without a waw, meaning: He created them as an adornment, so that you may ride them. Or ﴿زِينَةً﴾ may be taken as a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) from them, meaning: He created them for you to ride, and they are an adornment and beauty.

﴿وَيَخْلُقُ مَا لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ may mean: what He creates in us and for us of which we do not know the reality and details, and He bestows it upon us by mentioning it, just as He bestowed the known things, along with the indication of His power. It may also mean that He informs us that among His creatures are things of which we have no knowledge, in order to increase us in the evidence of His capability through this information, even though He has kept its knowledge hidden from us for a wisdom of His own in concealing it. It has also been interpreted as referring to what He has created in Paradise and Hell, which no one's imagination has reached and which has never occurred to any heart.

The meaning of "the way" (al-sabil) here is the category as a whole. That is why He attached to it "the direct" (al-qasd), and said: "and among them is the deviating one" (wa-minha ja'ir). Qasd is a verbal noun used in the sense of the active participle, meaning the one who goes straight (al-qasid). It is said: a straight way (sabil qasd) and a direct way (sabil qasid), that is, upright, as if it aims at the course that the traveler intends and does not turn away from. The meaning of His words: "And upon God is the direction of the way" is that guidance to the path that reaches the truth is obligatory upon Him, [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is that guidance to the path that reaches the truth is obligatory ... etc." Ahmad said: Where does he take it away from the continuation of the verse? That is His words: "And had He willed, He would have guided you all." If the matter were as the Qadariyya claim, the statement would have been: "And He has guided you all." And they are only believing in part of the Book and disbelieving in part. If they go to interpret guidance as compulsion and constraint, then they are only distorting the words from their places. As for the difference between the two styles, it is because the context of the speech is to establish the proof of God the Exalted against the creatures, by clarifying the direct way and the deviating way, and He guided a people who chose guidance, and He led astray a people who chose misguidance for themselves. It has been mentioned in more than one place that every act that proceeds through a servant has two considerations: it is, insofar as it exists, created by God the Exalted and is attributed to Him by this consideration; and it is, insofar as it is accompanied by the servant's choice of it and his ability to do it and its ease for him, attributed to the servant. The plurality of these two considerations is established in every act. So it was fitting, in establishing the proof against the servants, to attribute guidance to God the Exalted in respect of His creating it, and to attribute misguidance to the servant in respect of his choosing it. The conclusion is that He mentioned in each of the two acts an attribution different from the one mentioned in the other, so that this would suit the establishment of proof: "Say: To God belongs the conclusive proof" (Qul fa-lillahi al-hujjat al-baligha). And God is the One who grants success to what is right.]] obligatory upon Him, [[The words "the path that reaches the truth is obligatory upon Him": this is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila. There is no obligation upon God the Exalted according to the People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna); rather that is a favour from Him, but the Generous One presents the promise of good in the form of an obligation. (Ε)]] like His words: "Indeed, upon Us is the guidance" (Inna 'alayna lal-huda). If you say: why did the style of the speech change in His words "and among them is the deviating one"? I say: so that it may be known which of the two ways may be attributed to Him and which may not. And if the matter were as the Mujbira claim, [[The words "if the matter were as the Mujbira claim, it would be said: 'And upon God is the direction of the way'": this means the People of the Sunna, in that He the Exalted creates evil as He creates good. And his words "it would be said" etc.: the implication is rejected, because the Generous One loves good and not evil, even though each of them is from Him: "Say: Each is from God" (Qul kullun min 'indi Allah). (Ε)]] it would be said: "And upon God is the direction of the way, and upon Him is its deviating one," or "and upon Him is the deviating one." And 'Abdullah recited: "and among you is a deviating one" (wa-minkum ja'ir), meaning: and among you is a deviator who deviates from the direct way by his own bad choice, and God is free of him. "And had He willed, He would have guided you all" by compulsion and constraint. [[The words "And had He willed, He would have guided you all by compulsion and constraint": this is the position of the Mu'tazila. As for the People of the Sunna, He would have guided all by choice. That is because the Mu'tazila made it obligatory upon God to do what is best (al-salah), and guiding everyone is what is best, so the apparent sense of the verse contradicts their doctrine. Therefore they said: He intended to guide everyone, but it is an intention that does not conflict with the servant's free choice, lest his responsibility be nullified. And this intention does not entail that the intended thing occurs. The People of the Sunna do not make anything obligatory upon God the Exalted, and whatever God wills must occur. And this intention does not conflict, in their view, with the servant's choice, because of the acquisition (kasb) established for him, as is explained in the science of divine unity ('ilm al-tawhid). (Ε)]]

Lakum is related to anzala (He sent down), or, as a predicate of sharab (drink). Shajar means the trees that livestock graze on. In a report from Ikrimah: "Do not eat the price of trees, for it is unlawful gain" [Abu 'Ubayd related it in al-Amwal from him as a statement of his own (mawquf), and added something similar. 'Abd al-Razzaq related from the route of Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Beware of unlawful gain." They said: "And what is unlawful gain?" He said: "The sale of trees, the price of wine, and the hire of a female slave who engages in lesbianism."] That is, al-kala' (pasture): tusimuna (you pasture), from sāmat al-māshiyah when livestock grazed, so it is sa'imah, and its owner asāmahā; it derives from al-sawmah, which is the mark, because grazing leaves marks on the land.

It was read as yunbit (with ya' and nun). If you ask: why was it said "and of all the fruits"? I say: because all the fruits do not exist except in Paradise, and only some of them are caused to grow on earth as a reminder, [so that] yatafakkarun (they may reflect), looking and deducing through them His existence, His power and His wisdom.

The āyah means the clear proof. It is reported from some of them: yunbit, with tashdid (emphasis). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: yunbitu lakum bihi al-zar' wal-zaytun wal-nakhil wal-a'nab, in the nominative (marfu').

Qur'anic verse quoted: ﴿And He subjected to you the night and the day, and the sun and the moon; and the stars are subjected by His command.﴾ (Qur'an 16:12, as the commentary's quotation begins in the verse; the passage itself quotes only part of it.)

Translation:

It is read entirely in the accusative (naṣb), on the basis of: "and He made the stars subjected" (wa-ja'ala al-nujūma musakhkharāt). Or, on the basis that the meaning of their being subjected for people (taskhīruhā li-l-nās) is: making them beneficial to them, in that they find rest in the night, seek of His bounty by day, know the number of years and the reckoning by the movement of the sun and the moon, and find their way by the stars. It is as if it were said: "and He benefited you through them while they are subjected, created for what they were created for, by His command." It is also permissible that the meaning is: He subjected them in various kinds of subjection, the plural of musakhkhar, meaning taskhīr (subjection), from your saying "Allah subjected him (sakhkharahu Allāhu) to subjection (musakhkharan)," like your saying "he sent him away (sarraḥahu) to a sending away (misrāḥan)." It is as if it were said: "and He subjected them to you in subjections, by His command." It is also read with the accusative for "the night" and "the day" alone, while what follows them is in the nominative, as a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar).

It is also read: "and the stars are subjected" (wa-l-nujūmu musakhkharātun), in the nominative, while what precedes it is in the accusative. And He said: "Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason" (inna fī dhālika la-āyātin li-qawmin ya'qilūn), using the plural of āyah (sign). And reason is mentioned because the heavenly phenomena are the clearer evidence of overwhelming power, and the plainer testimony to majesty and greatness.
﴿And what He has created for you﴾ is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "the night and the day." It means: what He created in them of animals, trees, fruits, and other things of varied forms and appearances.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 14:

﴿لَحْمًا طَرِيًّا﴾ is fish, and he described it as fresh (ṭarī) because spoilage comes quickly to it, so one hastens to eat it for fear of its spoiling. [[His words "bi-l-ṭarāʾa" in al-Ṣiḥāḥ (of al-Jawharī): ṭaraw al-laḥm, and ṭarā ṭarāwa, ṭarāʾ and ṭarāʾa. (ʿ)]] [[He returned to his discussion, saying: "It is fish, and he described it as fresh because spoilage comes quickly to it..." etc. Aḥmad said: this seems to be an instruction about eating it and a guidance that it should only be consumed when fresh. The physicians say that consuming it after its freshness has gone is the most harmful thing, and God knows best.]] If you say: what is the matter with the jurists who say that if a man swears he will not eat meat (laḥm) and then eats fish, he does not break his oath, while God has called it "meat" as you see? I answer: the basis of oaths is custom, and people's custom, when "meat" is mentioned without qualification, is that fish is not understood from it; and if a man says to his servant, "Buy meat with these dirhams," and he brings fish, he deserves to be rebuked. An example of this is that God called the disbelievers "beasts" in His words: ﴿Indeed, the worst of beasts in the sight of God are those who disbelieve﴾; so if someone swore he would not ride a beast and then rode a disbeliever, he would not break his oath. ﴿Ornaments (ḥilyah) which they wear﴾: these are pearls and coral.

The intended meaning of ﴿their wearing﴾ is the wearing of their women, because they are part of them, and because they adorn themselves with these only for their sake, so they are, as it were, their adornment and clothing. al-Makhr: the cleaving of water with its breast. And on the authority of al-Farrāʾ: it is the sound of the ship's passage through the winds. And ﴿seeking His bounty﴾: trade.

Lest it sway with you (out of dislike that it should lean and shake with you). The one who is "māʾid" is the one who is made to sway when he rides the sea.

It was said: when God created the earth, it began to sway, so the angels said: "No one can settle on its back." Then in the morning it had been set firm with the mountains, and the angels did not know what it had been created from.

And rivers (anhāran), and He placed in it rivers, because alqā (to cast) carries the meaning of jaʿala (to place). Do you not see His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place, and the mountains as pegs?﴾

And landmarks (ʿalāmāt): these are the markers of the roads and everything by which travelers (al-sābila) guide themselves, such as a mountain, a watering place, and other things.

By "the star" (al-najm) is meant the genus, as when you say: "The dirham has become plentiful in people's hands." It is related from al-Suddi that it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā), the two Guards (al-Farqadān), the Daughters of the Bier (Banāt Naʿsh), and Polaris (al-Jadi).

Al-Hasan recited "wa-bi-l-najm" with two dammas, and with one damma and a sukun, and it is the plural of najm, like rahn and ruhn, and the sukun is a lightening. It was also said that the waw was dropped from al-nujūm for lightness.

If you say: the statement ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ departs from the customary style of address, with bi-l-najm placed first and hum inserted within it, as if it were said: "And by the star, specifically these, specifically they are guided." Then who is meant by hum? I say: it seems he meant the Quraysh. They had guidance by the stars in their travels, and they had a knowledge in this which was not the like of what others had, so gratitude was more obligatory upon them and reflection more binding on them, and so they were singled out.

Lest it sway with you (out of dislike that it should lean and shake with you). The one who is "māʾid" is the one who is made to sway when he rides the sea.

It was said: when God created the earth, it began to sway, so the angels said: "No one can settle on its back." Then in the morning it had been set firm with the mountains, and the angels did not know what it had been created from.

And rivers (anhāran), and He placed in it rivers, because alqā (to cast) carries the meaning of jaʿala (to place). Do you not see His saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place, and the mountains as pegs?﴾

And landmarks (ʿalāmāt): these are the markers of the roads and everything by which travelers (al-sābila) guide themselves, such as a mountain, a watering place, and other things.

By "the star" (al-najm) is meant the genus, as when you say: "The dirham has become plentiful in people's hands." It is related from al-Suddi that it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayyā), the two Guards (al-Farqadān), the Daughters of the Bier (Banāt Naʿsh), and Polaris (al-Jadi).

Al-Hasan recited "wa-bi-l-najm" with two dammas, and with one damma and a sukun, and it is the plural of najm, like rahn and ruhn, and the sukun is a lightening. It was also said that the waw was dropped from al-nujūm for lightness.

If you say: the statement ﴿and by the star they are guided﴾ departs from the customary style of address, with bi-l-najm placed first and hum inserted within it, as if it were said: "And by the star, specifically these, specifically they are guided." Then who is meant by hum? I say: it seems he meant the Quraysh. They had guidance by the stars in their travels, and they had a knowledge in this which was not the like of what others had, so gratitude was more obligatory upon them and reflection more binding on them, and so they were singled out.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 17:

If you say: "Who does not create" (kaman la yakhluqu) refers to the idols, [[Mahmud said: "If you say, 'Who does not create' is meant to refer to the idols... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This is a veiled reference to the claim that servants create their own actions, and that the purpose is to show the disparity between those among them who create and those who do not create, such as the incapacitated and the disabled, so that the disparity between those among them who create and the idols is established all the more so. Greed for this has taken hold of him to the point that he believes it establishes that the servant creates his actions, by interpreting the verse in this way, and he wishes that this had been fully established for him.

"And not everything a person wishes for does he attain."]] why then is "man" (alladhi li-ula al-'ilm, "the one for those of knowledge") used? I say:

There are several aspects. First: they named them "gods" and worshipped them, so they treated them as if they were of those endowed with knowledge. Do you not see His saying right after it: "And those whom they call upon besides Allah create nothing, and they themselves are created" (Qur'an 16:20). Second: the correspondence (mushakalah) between it and "who creates." Third: the meaning is that one who creates is not like one who does not create among those endowed with knowledge, so how much less is one who has no knowledge at all, like His saying: "Do they have feet with which they walk?" (Qur'an 7:195). The meaning is that the condition of the gods is lower than the condition of those who have feet, hands, ears and hearts, because those are living and they are dead, so how could worship be valid for them? Not that if these limbs were valid for them, worship would be valid for them. If you say: this is a rebuke to those who worshipped idols [[his speech ends. He said: "If you say, it is a rebuke to those who worshipped idols and named them gods, likening them to God Most High, and the rebuke should rightly say..." etc. Ahmad said: The discussion of this has already been covered at His saying "and the male is not like the female" (Qur'an 3:36), so renew your acquaintance with it.]] and they named them gods, likening them to Allah, then they have made what does not create like the Creator, so the rebuke should rightly be: "Is then the one who creates like the one who does not create?" I say: When they made other than Allah like Allah by naming it with His name and worshipping it, and equated it with Him, they have made Allah Most High of the same kind as created things and similar to them, so He rebuked them for that with His saying: "Is then the one who creates like the one who does not create?" Qur'anic quotations: ﴿Though you count the favours of Allah, you cannot number them.﴾ ... Let me translate directly.

"﴿And if you tried to count Allah's blessings, you could not enumerate them﴾" — "لا تُحْصُوها" means: you cannot keep count of them, nor can your capacity reach them, let alone your ability to fulfil their due through thanking Him. He follows that with a listing of His blessings, as a reminder that beyond them there is what cannot be restricted or counted.

﴿Indeed Allah is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾ — in that He overlooks your shortcoming in giving thanks for the blessing, does not cut it off from you because of your negligence, and does not hasten punishment upon you for your ingratitude.

﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you disclose﴾ — of your deeds; and this is a warning.

And those whom they call upon, namely the gods that the disbelievers invoke besides Allah. It is also recited with the taa' (تدعون, *tad'awna*). It is also recited as *yud'awna* in the passive voice (*al-bina' lil-maf'ul*).

He negated the attributes of divinity from them by negating that they are creators, that they are living and do not die, and that they know the time of resurrection. He affirmed for them the attributes of creation: that they are created, that they are dead, and that they are ignorant of the unseen. The meaning of ﴿أَمْوَاتٌ غَيْرُ أَحْيَاءٍ﴾ (dead, not living) is that if they were gods in reality, they would be living, not dead, meaning that death would not be permissible for them, like the living who does not die. Their condition is the reverse of this.

The pronoun in ﴿يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ (they are raised) refers to those who call upon them, meaning that they do not perceive when their worshippers will be raised. In this there is mockery of the polytheists, and that their gods do not know the time of their resurrection, so how could there be a time of reward from them for their worship? In it is also evidence that there must be a resurrection, and that it is a necessary consequence of moral obligation (*al-taklif*).

Another interpretation: the meaning is that people create them by carving and shaping, while they are unable to do such a thing. Thus they are more incapable than their worshippers. They are dead, lifeless stones with no life in them, ﴿غَيْرُ أَحْيَاءٍ﴾ meaning that among dead things there are those whose death is followed by life, like the drops of semen that Allah brings into being as animals, and the bodies of animals that will be raised after their death. As for stones, they are dead things whose death is not followed by life, and this is more emphatic in their deadness. ﴿وَمَا يَشْعُرُونَ أَيَّانَ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ (and they do not perceive when they will be raised) means: these gods do not know when the living will be raised, mocking their state, because the perception of inanimate matter is impossible. [[His saying, "because the perception of inanimate matter is impossible," means that its perception of what living beings perceive is impossible, so how much more impossible is its perception of what no living being knows except the Living, the Self-Subsisting (*al-Hayy al-Qayyum*), subhanahu, namely the time of resurrection. Perhaps there is a gap in the author's expression, and its intended sense is: the perception of inanimate matter of what living beings perceive. It is also recited as *iyyan* (إيان) with a kasra on the hamza.

Your God is One God. This means that it has been established, by what preceded it of refuting the notion that divinity belongs to anyone else, that divinity belongs to Him alone, with no partner in it. So the consequence of the firmness of Oneness and the clarity of its proof was that they persisted in their polytheism, and that their hearts denied Oneness, and that they were arrogant toward it and toward affirming it. "Undoubtedly (la jaram, haqqan) God knows what they conceal and what they reveal," so He will recompense them; and this is a threat. "Indeed, He does not love the arrogant." It is permissible that this refers to those arrogant toward monotheism, meaning the polytheists. It is also permissible that it encompasses every arrogant person, and these are included under its generality.

Ma (ماذا) is in the accusative, governed by anzala ("sent down"), meaning: "What is it that your Lord has sent down?" Or it is in the nominative, as the subject of an inceptive sentence, meaning: "What is it that your Lord has sent down?" [i.e., "What is the thing your Lord sent down?"]. If you read it in the accusative, the meaning of "asatir al-awwalin" ("tales of the ancients") is "what they claim was sent down is the tales of the ancients." If you read it in the nominative, the meaning is: "what was sent down is the tales of the ancients," like His words ﴿What is it that they spend?﴾ [Qur'an 2:219], according to the reading of those who put the word in the nominative, [answer:] ﴿Say: the surplus﴾ [Qur'an 2:219].

If you say: this is a self-contradictory statement, since it cannot be both "what your Lord sent down" and "tales of the ancients"? I reply: it is said in mockery, like the saying:

"Indeed your messenger [who was sent to you is truly mad]" [the note in the text: the verse is "Indeed your messenger who was sent to you is mad" (Qur'an 26:27)]. This is the speech of some of them to others, or the words of the Muslims to them. It is also said that it is the speech of the Muqtasimun (those who divided the approaches to Mecca):

They were those who divided the entrances of Mecca, turning people away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). When the delegations of pilgrims asked them about what had been sent down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they said: "The tales and falsehoods of the ancients," so that they would bear their burdens: that is, they said that to mislead people and to hinder them from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So they bore the full burden of their own misguidance, and a portion of the burdens of those whom they misled by their misguidance, namely the burden of misleading. For the one who misleads and the one who is misled are partners: this one misleads, and that one submits to his misleading, so both bear the burden. The lam (ل) in "liyahmilu" [expresses] causation without being a purpose, like your saying: "I left the town out of fear of harm." ﴿Without knowledge﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the object: that is, they mislead those who do not know that they are misguided. The people who were misled are described as misguided, and they bear the burden of those who misled them even if they did not know, because it was incumbent upon them to investigate and reflect with their intellect until they could distinguish between the truthful and the falsifier.

**al-Qawa'id** (the pillars): the columns that support the building. It is also said that it means the foundations. This is a figurative image. The meaning is that they set up structures in order to plot against Allah and His Messenger, so Allah made their destruction come through those very structures. This is like the case of a people who built a building and supported it with pillars, and then "the building came at them from its pillars, as its supports gave way, so the roof fell on them and they perished." A similar saying is: "Whoever digs a pit for his brother will fall into it headlong."

It is also said that this refers to Nimrod ibn Kan'an, when he built the tower in Babylon. Its height was five thousand cubits, and some say two farsakhs. So Allah sent a wind that toppled it upon him and his people, and they perished.

The meaning of "the coming of Allah" is the coming of His command "from the foundations," that is, from the direction of the foundations, "from where they did not perceive," meaning from where they did not expect or anticipate it.

It is also recited as *fa-ata Allahu bunyanahum* ("Allah came to their building"), and as *fa-kharra 'alayhimu al-saqfu* with both vowels marked (*al-suqfu*, a variant reading). "He will disgrace them" means He will humiliate them with the punishment of disgrace. "Our Lord, indeed whoever You cause to enter the Fire, You have certainly disgraced him." This means that this is their condition in this world, and then there is the punishment in the Hereafter.

"My partners" is an attribution to Himself, reporting their own attribution, in order to rebuke them with it in a mocking manner. "You used to oppose them": you used to be hostile to and dispute with the believers regarding them and their affair. It is also recited as *tushaqqūna* with a kasra on the nun (*tushāqqūnī*, "you oppose Me"), because opposing the believers is as though it were opposing Allah.

"Those who were given knowledge" are the prophets and the scholars among their communities, who used to call them to faith and admonish them, but they paid them no heed, behaved arrogantly toward them and opposed them. They say this out of gloating over them. Allah relates this statement of theirs so that it may serve as a lesson (*lutf*, a kindness that guides) for whoever hears it. It is also said that they are the angels.

It is recited as *tatawaffāhum* with a tā' or a yā' (both forms).

It is also recited as *alladhīna tawaffāhumu* with the tā' assimilated into the tā' (*idgham*, assimilation of consonants).

"Then they offered peace": they submitted and humbled themselves, and they came with the opposite of what they had been upon in the world, of opposition and arrogance. They said: "We were not doing any evil," and they denied the disbelief and transgression that had been found in them. So "those who had knowledge" replied to them: "Indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do," meaning He will repay you for it. This is also a form of gloating. Likewise, "Enter the gates of Hell."

"Then they offered peace": they submitted and humbled themselves, and they came with the opposite of what they had been upon in the world, of opposition and arrogance. They said: "We were not doing any evil," and they denied the disbelief and transgression that had been found in them. So "those who had knowledge" replied to them: "Indeed Allah is Knowing of what you used to do," meaning He will repay you for it. This is also a form of gloating. Likewise, "Enter the gates of Hell."

Why is this (khayran) in the accusative (naṣb), while the first one is in the nominative (raf')? I say: they are separated by the answer of the one who acknowledges (al-muqirr) and the answer of the one who denies (al-jahid). The meaning is that these people, when they were asked, did not hesitate, but answered the question directly and plainly, making what was sent down the object of "anzala" (sent down), so they said "khayran" (good), meaning "He sent down good." Those others, however, evaded the question and said, "It is only the fables of the ancients" (﴿أَسَاطِيرُ الْأَوَّلِينَ﴾), which has nothing to do with sending down.

It is related that the tribes of the Arabs used to send, during the season of pilgrimage (al-mawsim), someone to bring them news of the Prophet (ﷺ). When the delegate (al-wafid) arrived, the dividers (al-muqtasimun) would stop him and order him to turn back, saying: "If you do not meet him, it will be better for you." He would reply: "I would be the worst delegate if I returned to my people without finding out the matter of Muhammad and seeing him." So he would meet the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and they would inform him of his truthfulness and that he was a prophet sent by God. These are the ones who said "khayran."

As for His saying ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا﴾ and what follows it, it is a substitute (badal) for "khayran," as a report of His saying ﴿لِلَّذِينَ اتَّقَوْا﴾, meaning: they said this statement. The naming of it as "good" came first, and then it was reported.

It is also permissible for it to be a new, independent sentence (kalam mubtada'), meaning the words of those who said it, and their statement is considered part of their good deeds, and they are praised for it. ﴿لِلَّذِينَ أَحْسَنُوا فِي هَذِهِ الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةٌ﴾ is a recompense in this world for their good deeds, and ﴿وَلَدَارُ الْآخِرَةِ خَيْرٌ﴾ is for them in the Hereafter, which is better than it, like His saying: ﴿فَآتَاهُمُ اللَّهُ ثَوَابَ الدُّنْيَا وَحُسْنَ ثَوَابِ الْآخِرَةِ﴾. And ﴿وَلَنِعْمَ دَارُ الْمُتَّقِينَ﴾ means the Abode of the Hereafter, so the object of praise (al-mukhassas bi-l-madh) has been omitted because it was already mentioned. ﴿جَنَّاتُ عَدْنٍ﴾ is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada').

because they did what made destruction their due. ﴿The evil deeds of what they had done befell them﴾: the recompense for the evil of their deeds. Or it is like His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾.

This is among the list of the kinds of their disbelief and obstinacy: their association of partners with God, their denial of His oneness after the proofs had been established, their denial of resurrection and their urging for it to be hastened, their mockery of him, their denial of the Messenger, their opposition, and their arrogance in refusing to accept the truth. That is: they associated partners with God and declared unlawful what God had made lawful, such as the *baḥīra* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and was released), the *sā'iba* (a freed animal) and others. Then they attributed their deed to God and said: ﴿If God had willed, we would not have done it﴾. This is exactly the doctrine of the *Mujbira* (Jabriyya, those who hold that man has no real power over his acts) [[The statement "and they said: If God had willed, we would not have done it, and this is exactly the doctrine of the Mujbira" means Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna). It is not as he said. Rather, the polytheists said it mockingly, while Ahl al-Sunna hold it as a belief, as al-Nasafi has stated. Whatever God wills comes to be, and whatever He does not will does not come to be, whether it is evil or good. Every matter is by His decree and destiny, whether evil or good. He is the Creator of the acts of the servants, even though they are by their acquisition (*kasb*) and choice, in contrast to the Mu'tazila in all of that, as he extensively argued later here in defence of the Mu'tazila. (ʿ)]] Likewise did those before them, that is, they associated partners and declared unlawful what God had made lawful [[Mahmud said: "That is, they associated partners with God and declared unlawful what God had made lawful..." etc. Ahmad says: he has repeated a similar section of this kind in the counterpart of the preceding verse in Surat al-An'am, and we had already presented there what is sufficient, God willing. What he has added here establishes his doctrine according to his own claim, by the words of God the Exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger, [saying]: Worship God and avoid the Taghut﴾. The way he holds this as evidence is that God the Exalted divided worship into two parts: what is commanded and what is forbidden. The command and the prohibition, according to the author, return to the will, based on the claim of the Qadariyya in denying the inner speech (*kalam al-nafs*) and interpreting the demand as will. The conclusion, then, from this supplement is that God willed the creatures' worship of Him and willed their avoidance of worshipping the Taghut, and did not will for them that they should associate partners with Him, and He informed of this will through the tongue of every messenger He sent to a nation among the nations. So the supplement came as a translation of the meaning of the opening of the verse, confirming its implication. This is what the author added here, and we have shown that its basis is the denial of inner speech, which is established with certainty, so it is categorically false. What is astonishing is that God the Exalted made clear in both verses that what He denied of the speakers of ﴿If God had willed, we would not have associated [anything with Him]﴾ is only their argument against God by His will, for which they have no proof, along with the faculty of choice He created for them, by His words here: ﴿So among them are those whom God guided, and among them are those upon whom error was justly decreed﴾, and by His words at the end of the verse of al-An'am: ﴿Then to God belongs the conclusive argument; so if He had willed, He would have guided you all﴾. Thus it became clear in both that He is the One who willed for them association and misguidance, and had He willed their guidance, they would all have been guided without exception. From this explanation there results the diversion of the denunciation toward them rather than attributing the will to God the Exalted, and this is what we had mentioned in their establishing the argument against God by His will, even though their argument in that is void, and God's is the conclusive and manifest proof. And God is the Granter of success.]], then when they were warned about the ugliness of their deed, they attributed it (to God) [[His words "and they attributed it to their Lord" means they accused Him of it. (ʿ)]]. So upon the Messengers is only to convey the truth, and to make clear, by explanation and proof, that God does not will polytheism and sins, and to make known the falsehood and ugliness of polytheism and the freedom of God the Exalted from the acts of the servants, and that they perform these acts by their own intention, will and choice, while God the Exalted is the one who motivates them toward what is good, enables them to do it, restrains them from what is ugly, and promises reward for it.

This passage is part of al-Zamakhshari's (d. 538 AH) commentary, al-Kashshaf, a work of Mu'tazili rationalist tafsir. The term "lutf" (divine grace or favour that makes obedience more likely) is central here, so I translate it as such.

And indeed He has strengthened the refutation of the belief that evil is decreed and that the will of evil is from Him, by [stating] that there is no community except that a messenger has been sent among them, commanding them to the good, which is faith and the worship of God, and to avoid evil, which is obedience to the tyrant (taghut). ﴿So among them were those whom God guided﴾, meaning He showed them grace (lutf), because He knew them to be among those fit for grace; ﴿and among them were those upon whom error was justly due﴾, meaning that abandonment (khidhlan) was confirmed upon him, and withholding of grace, because He knew him to be fixed in disbelief, from whom no good would come. ﴿So travel through the earth and observe what was the end of the deniers﴾, so that you have no doubt that I do not decree evil nor will it, in that I act as I act with the wicked.

Then he mentions the obstinacy of the Quraysh and the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ eagerness for their faith, and informs him that they are among the group upon whom misguidance is decreed, and that He does not guide whoever He leaves astray, meaning He does not show kindness (lutf) to one whom He forsakes, because that would be pointless, and Allah the Exalted is above pointlessness, since it belongs to the category of ugly acts that are not permissible for Him. It is also read: ﴿lā yuhdā﴾ [[His saying "and it is read: lā yuhdā" means in the passive voice, as Al-Nasafi explained. (Ghayn)]], meaning: neither you nor anyone else can guide him, since Allah has forsaken him. His saying ﴿wa-mā lahum min nāṣirīn﴾ ("and they have no helpers") is evidence that what is meant by "leading astray" is forsaking, which is the opposite of granting victory. It is also permissible that ﴿lā yahdī﴾ means "does not become guided," as one says: "Allah guided him, so he was guided." In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿fa-inna Allāha lā hādiya liman yuḍall, wa-liman aḍall﴾ ("indeed Allah has no guide for whom He leads astray, and for whom He has led astray"), which supports those who read ﴿lā yuhdā﴾ in the passive voice. In the reading of ʿAbd Allāh: ﴿yahtadī﴾ with the tā' of yahtadī assimilated, which supports the first reading. It is also read ﴿yuḍall﴾ with a fatḥah. And al-Nakhaʿī read ﴿in taḥriṣ﴾ with a fatḥah on the rāʾ, which is a dialectal form.

And they swear by Allah with their most solemn oaths: (this is) coordinated with "those who associated partners [with Allah] said," signifying that these are two great disbelieves, described as truly deserving to be related and recorded: (namely) their attributing their sins to the will of Allah [[His saying "attributing their sins to the will of Allah" means: relating their sins to His will, and accusing Him of them. (Ṭ)]], and their denial of resurrection, swearing to it. "Balā" (Yes indeed) is an affirmation of what follows the negation, i.e., "Yes indeed, He will resurrect them." "Waʿd Allāh" (the promise of Allah) is a verbal noun emphasizing what "balā" implies: that resurrection is a promise from Allah, and it makes clear that fulfilling this promise is a binding truth upon Him by wisdom. (Ṭ)]], because they say: nothing is binding upon Allah, neither the reward of the doer nor any other of the requirements of wisdom. Qawluna (our saying) is the subject (mubtada'), and an-naqula (that We say) is its predicate (khabar). Kun fa-yakun: kāna here is the complete verb (kān al-tāmma), meaning "to come into being, to exist." The sense is: when We intend the existence of a thing, there is nothing more than that We say to it, "Come into being," and it comes into being immediately after that, without any delay. This is an illustration that what He wills cannot elude Him, and that its existence at the moment of His will, may He be exalted, is not contingent on anything, like the existence of what is commanded at the order of an obeyed commander when it reaches an obedient subordinate who complies. There is no actual saying here (wa-la qawla thumma). The meaning is that the bringing into being of every created thing is with God, may He be exalted, this easy, so how could the resurrection, which is one of the things within the scope of His power, be beyond Him?

It is also recited as fa-yakūnu, in the form of a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon naqūlu.

﴿وَالَّذِينَ هاجَرُوا﴾ refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions. The people of Makkah oppressed them, so they fled with their religion to Allah. Some of them emigrated to Abyssinia and then to Madinah, thus combining the two migrations. Others emigrated directly to Madinah. It was also said that they are those who were detained and tortured after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had emigrated, and whenever they went out, the Makkans pursued them and brought them back. Among them were Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, and ʿAmmar. It is related from Suhayb that he said to them: "I am an old man. If I am with you, I will not benefit you, and if I am against you, I will not harm you." So he ransomed himself from them with his wealth and emigrated. When Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) saw him, he said: "The sale has profited, O Suhayb." ʿUmar said to him: "What an excellent man Suhayb is! If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." This is a great praise, meaning: if Allah had not created Hell, he would still obey Him. [[The statement "if Allah had not created Hell, he would still obey Him, so how much more..." means: how then would he not obey Him? Yet Allah created it for those who disobey. (ʿ)]]

﴿فكيف فِي اللَّهِ في حقه ولوجهه حَسَنَةً﴾ is an adjective (ṣifah) describing the verbal noun (maṣdar), i.e., "a good dwelling" (tabwi'ah ḥasanah). In the recitation (qira'ah) of ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), it is read as "linathwiyannahum," and its meaning is: "a good abode." It was also said: "We will settle them in this world in a good position," which is dominance over the people of Makkah who oppressed them, over all the Arabs, and over the people of the East and the West. It is related from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that whenever he gave a grant to a man from the Emigrants, he would say: "Take it, may Allah bless it for you. This is what your Lord promised you in this world, and what He has stored for you in the Hereafter is greater."

It was also said: "We will settle them in a good dwelling (mubāʾah ḥasanah)," which is Madinah, where its people sheltered them and supported them.

﴿لَوْ كانُوا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾: the pronoun refers to the disbelievers, meaning: if they knew that Allah gathers for these weak ones both this world and the Hereafter, they would desire their religion. It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to the Emigrants, meaning: if they knew that, they would increase their striving and patience.

﴿الَّذِينَ صَبَرُوا﴾ on: either it is "they are those who were patient," or it is "I mean those who were patient," and both are praise, meaning: they were patient under torture and in leaving the homeland, which is the sanctuary of Allah, beloved in every heart, so how much more so in the hearts of a people for whom it is the place of their birth; and they were patient in striving and in giving up their lives in the way of Allah.

Among them were Bilal, Suhayb, Khabbab, and ʿAmmar. It is related from Suhayb that he said to them: "I am an old man. If I am with you, I will not benefit you, and if I am against you, I will not harm you." So he ransomed himself from them with his wealth and emigrated. When Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) saw him, he said: "The sale has profited, O Suhayb." ʿUmar said to him: "What an excellent man Suhayb is! If he did not fear Allah, he would not disobey Him." This is a great praise, meaning: if Allah had not created Hell, he would still obey Him. [[The statement "if Allah had not created Hell, he would still obey Him, so how much more..." means: how then would he not obey Him? Yet Allah created it for those who disobey. (ʿ)]]

In the recitation (qira'ah) of ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), it is read as "linathwiyannahum," and its meaning is: "a good abode." It was also said: "We will settle them in this world in a good position," which is dominance over the people of Makkah who oppressed them, over all the Arabs, and over the people of the East and the West. It is related from ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) that whenever he gave a grant to a man from the Emigrants, he would say: "Take it, may Allah bless it for you. So it was said: ﴿We sent not before you except men to whom We revealed, through the tongues of the angels.﴾ ﴿So ask the people of the Reminder, if you do not know﴾, and they are the People of the Book, so that they may inform you that God did not send to the earlier nations except human beings.

Recited: "Awa lam yaraw" and "yatafayya'u" with the ya' and the ta'. "Ma" is a relative pronoun linked to "khalaqa Allah," and its explanation is indefinite: "min shay'in yatafayya'u zilaluhu." "Al-yamin" means "al-ayman" (the right sides).

"Sujjadan" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-zilal." "Wa hum dakhirun" is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "zilaluhu," because it has the meaning of the plural, namely "mā khalaqa Allāh min kulli shay'in lahu zill." It is pluralized with the waw, because "al-dukhur" is one of the attributes of rational beings, or because among that whole group there are those who reason, so the masculine was given precedence.

The meaning: "Have they not seen what God has created of bodies that have shadows which turn from their right and left sides," that is, from the two sides of each one of them. The phrase "shiqqayhi" is a metaphor, taken from the right and left of a person, for the two sides of a thing. That is: the shadows return from side to side, submitting to God, not resisting Him in what He has subjected them to of turning. The bodies themselves are also "dakhirun," humbled and submissive to God's actions upon them, not refusing.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verses 49–50:

"Min dabbah" (of any moving creature) may be an explanation of what is in the heavens and what is on the earth together, on the basis that there are creatures of God in the heavens who crawl about in them as human beings crawl on the earth. It may also be an explanation of what is on the earth alone, with "what is in the heavens" meaning the angels. He repeated their mention with the meaning: "and the angels in particular, among those who prostrate, because they are the most obedient and the most devoted of creation." It is also permissible that "what is in the heavens" means their angels.

By His saying "and the angels," it means the angels of the earth, including the guardian angels and others. If you say: the prostration of the morally responsible (mukallafun) is different from the prostration of others, and this speech encompasses both, [[Mahmud said: "If you say the prostration of the morally responsible is covered by this speech and is different from the prostration of others, how does it express the two types with one word...?" Ahmad said: This is what those who choose that a single word covers both its literal and figurative meanings comprehensively, without that being contradictory, hold on to. For prostration applies to the literal state of the morally responsible and, by way of figurative comparison (majaz al-tashbih), applies to the state of non-responsible beings, and both were intended by the verse. Al-Zamakhshari rejects this in places I have passed through in his book. Yet the apparent intent here is that prostration is an expression for a common quality shared between the act of the responsible and the state of non-responsible beings, namely non-refusal according to the Qadariyya. His aim in this is that the word be univocal (mutawati') in both, so as to avoid combining the literal and the figurative, since he rejects that. This aim is not realized in the verse, God knows best, because its being a verse of prostration indicates that the prostration mentioned in it, when attributed to the responsible, is the specific act customary in the Law (shar'an), whose mention is a cause for the customary prostration at the obligatory prostration verses (azaʾim al-sujud), not the more general common quality. God knows best.]] So how does it express the two types with one word? I say: what is meant by the prostration of the responsible is their obedience and worship, and by the prostration of others is their submission to the will of God and their not being able to resist it. Both prostrations share the meaning of submission, so they do not differ, and therefore it is permissible to express both with one word. If you say:

Why was "man" not used instead of "ma," to give precedence to the rational among the moving creatures over the others? I say: because if "man" had been used, there would have been no indication of the precedence, and it would have covered only the rational beings specifically. So what is suitable for both the rational and others was used, intending generality.

"Yakhafuna" (they fear) may be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "la yastakbiruna" (they do not wax proud), meaning: they do not wax proud while fearing. It may also be an explanation of the negation of pride and an emphasis of it, because whoever fears God does not become proud of worshipping Him. [[Mahmud said: "It may be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun ... etc." Ahmad said: This second is the correct view, not the first. As for the circumstantial clause, it gives the sense of transition (intiqal), and it suggests restricting the negation of pride to a condition, whereas the actual fact is that the absence of their pride is absolute and not restricted by any condition. And God is the Granter of success.]]

"Min fawqihim" (above them): if you attach it to "yakhafuna," the meaning is: they fear Him lest He send down punishment upon them from above them. If you attach it to "their Lord" as a circumstantial clause from Him, the meaning is: they fear their Lord, exalted over them, dominant over them, as in His saying ﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants﴾ and ﴿And indeed We are dominant over them﴾. In this is evidence that the angels are morally responsible, subject to command, prohibition, promise and threat like all responsible beings, and that they are between fear and hope.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 51:

If you say: they combine the number and the counted noun only beyond "one" and "two," saying "ʿindī rijāl thalātha" (I have three men) and "afrās arbaʿa" (four horses), because the counted noun, on its own, carries no indication of a specific number. But "rajul" (a man), "rajulān" (two men), "faras" (a horse) and "fārasān" (two horses) each already indicate a number, so there is no need to say "rajul wāḥid" (one man) or "rajulān ithnān" (two men, two). What then is the purpose of His saying ﴿ilāhayn ithnayn﴾ (two gods, two)? [[Maḥmūd said: "If you ask what is the benefit of His saying 'ithnayn' (two) when the dual form already suffices without it... etc." Aḥmad said: This section is one of its virtues which cannot be disputed, and God is the Granter of success.]]

I say: the noun that carries the meaning of singularity or duality indicates two things: the category (jinsiyya) and the specific number. When one wishes to indicate that the number is the thing intended, and that the discourse is directed toward it, it is reinforced with something that confirms it, and thereby it is shown that this is what is aimed at and cared for. Do you not see that if you said "innamā huwa ilāh" (He is only a god) without confirming it with "wāḥid" (one), it would not be good, and it would seem that you were affirming divinity, not unity?

﴿Fa-iyyāya fa-rhabūn﴾ (so fear Me, and Me alone) is a shift in the discourse from the third person (ghayba) to the first person (takallum). This is permissible because the speaker is the predominant one, and it is from the method of iltifāt (shift of address), and it is more forceful in instilling awe than his saying "wa-iyyāhu fa-rhabūhu" (and fear Him), and more forceful than if what precedes it had come in the form of the first person.

Al-Zamakhshari's commentary on Surah 16, verse 52:

"Al-din" (religion, obedience) — "wasiban" is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) whose governing element is the adverbial phrase (ẓarf). "Al-wāṣib" means the obligatory and the established, because every blessing comes from Him, so obedience is owed to Him by every person who receives a blessing. It is also permissible that it derives from "al-waṣab" (hardship, fatigue), meaning: and to Him belongs the religion as something burdensome and laborious, and for this reason it is called taklif (imposed obligation). Or: and to Him belongs the recompense, lasting, perpetual, everlasting, not ceasing, meaning the reward and the punishment.

Whatever blessing you have is from God. ﴿And whatever blessing you have is from God﴾. Whatever befalls you, or reaches you, of blessing, is from God. ﴿Then to Him you cry for help﴾, so you only supplicate to Him. Al-ju'ar (raising the voice in supplication and appeal for help) is raising the voice in du'a and istighatha (calling for aid).

al-A'sha said, describing a monk:

[[He alternates in the prayers to the King, at one time prostrating and at another time crying out in supplication.
And I do not know of anyone greater than him in piety when the reckoning comes, when the breezes shake off the dust.

By al-A'sha. Al-Aabali is the monk, attributed to Aabil, who was the keeper of the church. Al-haykal is the house of an idol. Salib: that is, the image of the cross.

The alif in sara is for lengthening (iṭlāq). Yurawih is its predicate, though this requires tadmin (the grammatical device of one verb carrying the sense of another) for the sake of the eloquence of the meaning. Al-murawaha in action is moving from one state to another. Al-salawat are the supplications. Al-sujud is lowering oneself and humility. Al-ju'ar is raising the voice in supplication. Bi-a'zam is the predicate of al-Aabali. Taqan is a tamyiz (specification of ambiguity). He says: the monk who devotes himself in his house, in which he has fashioned the cross, and who keeps moving and shifting from one supplication to God to another, sometimes prostrating himself and sometimes crying out, his piety is greater than your piety on the Day of Reckoning, when people rise from their graves and the dust shakes them off, a kinaya (metonymic allusion) for that.]]

It is also read ﴿tajarun﴾ with the hamza dropped and its vowel placed on the jim. Qatada read ﴿kashif al-darr﴾ (the one who removes harm) in the form fa'il in the sense of fa'ala, and it is stronger than kashafa, because the pattern of mughalaba (the form denoting contest or intensity) indicates intensification.

Sibawayh mentions al-an'am (the livestock) in the chapter on nouns that are not declined (*ghayr munṣarif*, diptotes) among singular nouns that follow the pattern of verbs, as in their saying: *thawb akyash* (a garment with a worn, ragged look). Therefore the pronoun referring back to it is singular. As for *fī buṭūnihā* in Surat al-Mu'minun, it is because its meaning is plural. It is permissible to say two things about *al-an'am* in this verse. The first is that it is a broken plural (*taksīr*) of *ni'am*, like *ajbāl* being the broken plural of *jabal*. The second is that it is a singular noun that carries the meaning of plurality, like *ni'am*. When it is treated as masculine, it is treated the way *ni'am* is treated in the line:

[[Note by the editor: "أن يكون تكثير نعم" is probably "تكسير" with an s. (ʿ)]]

*fī kulli ʿāmin niʿamun taḥwūnahu* ... *yulqiḥuhu qawmun wa-tantijūnah*
*arbābuhu nawkā fa-lā yaḥmūnahu* ... *wa-lā yulāqūna ṭiʿānan dūnah*
*anʿamu l-abnāʾi taḥsabūnahu* ... *hayhāta hayhāta limā tarjūnah*

(In every year there are camels that you gather, / a people mate them and you deliver their young. / Their owners are fools, so they do not protect them, / nor do they face spear-thrusts in defending them. / Do you think the camels are the camels of the boys? / Far, far is what you hope for.)

The poem is by a boy from Banu Asad named Qays ibn al-Husayn al-Harithi.

*Al-niʿam* is a collective noun (*ism jamʿ*) that is treated as singular, though its meaning is sometimes taken into account and it is treated as plural. Sibawayh counted *al-anʿām* among the singular nouns built on the pattern of plurals of the *afʿāl* type, like *akhlāq* and *amshāj*. So it is treated as masculine at times, in view of its form, and as feminine at other times, in view of its meaning. It has also been said that it is a plural of *niʿam*, like *asbāb* being the plural of *sabab*. The statement is one of regret and sorrow in the form of a report. It is possible to supply an interrogative hamza of rebuke or wonder before *fī*, meaning: "Do you do that every year?" It is also reported as *a-kulla ʿāmin* with the interrogative hamza.

*Kulla* is in the accusative as an adverb of time (*ẓarfiyya*). In it there is a report of time concerning a concrete noun, namely *niʿam*. This is either because it resembles the meaning, since it recurs every year, as Ibn Malik and others said about similar cases, or because of an implied noun, as the majority of the Basran grammarians held, meaning: "the plunder of camels."

The clause *taḥwūnahu* is an attribute of *niʿam*. It may also be its predicate. *Kull ʿām* is an adverbial complement of *taḥwūnahu* and was placed first because it is the focus of the question.

On this basis, what permits beginning with *niʿam* is that it falls within the scope of the interrogative. Or the fronting of the complement of the predicate before it, since it is like fronting the predicate.

*Yulqiḥuhu qawm* means they let its stallion mate with its females, so they become pregnant in their possession. *Tantijūnahu antum* means you yourselves bring it to birth among you, a metaphor for plundering it from them. *Al-arbāb* are the owners (*al-aṣḥāb*). *Al-nawkā* is the plural of *anwak*, like *ḥamqā* is the plural of *aḥmaq* in pattern and meaning. *Al-ṭiʿān* means fighting with spears, that is, they do not fight in front of it and do not endure battle.

His saying *anʿam* is a rebuking interrogative of denial, meaning: do not think that our camels are the camels of those weak fools.

*Hayhāt* means "far," and he repeated it for emphasis and to cut off hopes. His saying *limā tarjūnah* is governed by an implied element, meaning: I say that because of what you hope for, and the *lām* in it indicates the agent (*li-tabyīn al-fāʿil*). It is also permissible that the *lām* is superfluous in it. *Al-rajāʾ* is hope (*al-ṭamaʿ*), and it may also mean supposition (*al-ẓann*).

When it is treated as feminine, there are two possibilities: that it is a broken plural of *niʿam*, and that it carries the meaning of the plural.

It is read as *nusqīkum* with a fatḥa and with a ḍamma. It is a resumptive sentence (*istiʾnāf*), as if it were said: "What is the lesson?" and then it was said: *nusqīkum min bayni farthin wa-damin*, meaning: God creates milk as an intermediary between the dung and the blood that enclose it, and between it and them there is a barrier of God's power, so that neither of the two oppresses it with color, taste or smell, but it is pure of all that.

It has been said: when the beast eats fodder and it settles in its paunch, it cooks it. Its lowest part becomes dung, its middle part becomes milk, and its highest part becomes blood. The liver is set over these three categories, dividing them: it sends the blood through the veins and the milk into the udder, and the dung remains in the paunch.

Glory be to God, how great is His power and how subtle His wisdom to one who reflects and contemplates. Shaqiq was asked about sincerity (*al-ikhlāṣ*) and said: it is distinguishing the deed from its defects, like distinguishing milk from between dung and blood, smooth and easy to pass through the throat.

It is said: no one has ever choked on milk. It is read *sayʾan* with shadda, and *sayʾan* with the lightened form, like *hayyin* and *layyin*.

If you ask: what is the difference between the first *min* and the second? I say: the first is partitive (*littabʿīḍ*), because the milk is a part of what is in their bellies, as when you say: "I took a garment from Zayd's property." The second indicates the starting point (*libtidāʾ al-ghāya*), because between the dung and the blood is the place of the watering from which it begins. So it is attached to *nusqīkum*, as when you say: "I watered him from the pool." It is also permissible that it is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from *laban*, placed before it, so it is attached to an implied element, meaning: "being from between dung and blood."

Do you not see that if it were delayed and it said *laban min bayni farthin wa-dam*, it would be an attribute of it? It was placed first because it is the locus of the lesson, so it deserves to be placed first.

Some who hold that semen is pure have argued against those who consider it impure, using this verse, because it passes through the path of urine. They say it is not strange that something should pass through the path of urine while being pure, just as milk came out from between dung and blood while being pure.

The element was elided because "nusqikum" (We give you to drink) mentioned before it indicates it. The words "tattakhidhuna minhu sakaran" (you take from it an intoxicant) are an explanation and disclosure of the true nature of the giving of drink. Alternatively, it may relate to "tattakhidhuna," and the repetition of the adverbial phrase "minhu" (from it) is for emphasis, like your saying: "Zayd is in the house, in it."

It is also permissible that "tattakhidhuna" be a qualifier of an elided noun, as in the verse of the poet:

"... with a hand that was among the most skilled of people in archery" [[I have nothing with me but a whip and a stone, ... and no bow with a thick belly and a tight string.

[[The explanation of this evidence was given earlier in this part, p. 395; refer to it if you wish. Its corrector.]]

(ʿ)]] [[His saying "fa-qala: tanawalathu al-di'ara" (he said: corruption took hold of it): in al-Sihah, "al-di'ara" is wickedness and depravity. (ʿ)]] It is also said: "sakar" is the food. He recited:

"I made the honor of the noble into sakar"

meaning: I moved about with their honor [[in al-Sihah: "al-naql" with a damma is what one moves about with over drink. (ʿ)]]. The revelation to the bee: its inspiration, the casting of it into its heart, and its instruction in a manner that He knows best, and to which no one has any access. Otherwise, its skill in its craft, its subtlety in managing its affairs, and its accuracy in what benefits it are clear proofs that Allah deposited in it knowledge of this and gave it understanding, just as He gave people of reason their reason.[[The phrase "وإلا فنيقتها" means its *ta'annuq*, i.e. its skill. It is also read *buyūtan* with a kasra on the bāʾ for the sake of the following yāʾ.
