Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 16, verse 72:

﴿مِنْ أَنْفُسِكُمْ﴾: from your own kind. It is also said: this refers to the creation of Hawwa' (Eve) from a rib of Adam. The *hafadah* (ḥafadah, helpers/attendants) is the plural of *ḥāfid*, one who *yaḥfid*, that is, who hastens in obedience and service. From this is the saying of the one who recites the qunut: "And to You we hasten and serve."

And he said:

"He hastened the young maidservants among them, and they handed over the reins of the camels to their palms."

*Ḥafada* is of the *ḍaraba* pattern, meaning he hastened. *Al-walā'id* is the plural of *walīdah*, a young girl. *Baynahunna* means among the women who ride in the litters. *Uslimat* is in the passive voice, meaning it was left in the palms of the litter-riders and the maidservants. *Azimmat al-ajmāl* is the plural of *zimām* (rein), and this indicates their protection and guarding, such that no one touches their riding-beasts except the maidservants.

There is disagreement about who the *ḥafadah* are. It is said: they are the in-laws through daughters (*al-akhtān ʿalā al-banāt*). Regarding this statement, in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (al-Ṣiḥāḥ, the lexicon of al-Jawharī) it says: "*al-ḥafadah* are helpers and servants." It also says: "*al-khabn*, with a vowel on the first letter, is everyone who is on the side of the woman, such as the father and brother, and they are the *akhtān*; this is the usage of the Arabs. But among the common people, *khatn* is the husband of a man's daughter." Thus he may have also taken *al-akhtān* in the sense of *al-aʿwān* (helpers) or *al-khulafāʾ* (successors), so he connected it with *ʿalā*. In *al-Khāzin*, on the authority of Ibn Masʿūd: "*al-ḥafadah* are a man's in-laws through his daughters." (ʿ)

It is also said: they are the grandchildren. It is also said: they are the children of the woman from her first husband. It is also said: the meaning is "and He made for you *ḥafadah*," that is, servants who hasten in your affairs and assist you. It is also permissible that *al-ḥafadah* refers to the sons themselves, as in His saying ﴿سَكَراً وَرِزْقاً حَسَناً﴾ (16:67), as if it were said: "And He made for you from them children who are sons and who are *ḥāfidūn*," that is, combining both qualities.

﴿مِنَ الطَّيِّبَاتِ﴾: he means some of them, because all the good things are in Paradise, and the good things of this world are only a model of them.

﴿أَفَبِالْبَاطِلِ يُؤْمِنُونَ﴾: that is, what they believe about the benefit, blessing and intercession of the idols. This is nothing but a baseless illusion, for which they have not reached any proof or sign. So they have no faith except in it, as if it were something known and certain.

﴿وَنِعْمَةِ اللَّهِ﴾: the manifest, observed blessing about which there is no doubt for anyone with intellect and discernment. They disbelieve in it and deny it, just as one denies an impossibility that the intellect cannot conceive.

It is also said: *al-bāṭil* is what Satan adorns for them, such as the prohibition of the *baḥīrah* and the *sāʾibah* and others. And "the blessing of God" is what He made lawful for them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 73:

Al-rizq (provision) may be used in the sense of the verbal noun (maşdar), and in the sense of that which is provided (mā yurzaq). If you mean the verbal noun, you put "shay'an" (anything) in the accusative governed by it, as in His saying ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger, an orphan﴾ [90:14–15], according to the reading that makes it govern the accusative: "[they] do not possess the power to provide anything." If you mean the provided thing, then "shay'an" is a substitute (badal) for it, in the sense of "a little." It is also permissible for it to be an emphatic (ta'kid) for "lā yamlik," meaning: "they do not possess any part of the dominion."

As for ﴿and from the heavens and the earth﴾: it is connected (ṣilah) to "al-rizq" if it is a verbal noun, meaning: "they do not provide rain from the heavens, nor vegetation from the earth." Or it is a qualifier (ṣifah) if it is a noun for that which is provided.

The pronoun in ﴿and they are not able﴾ refers back to "mā," because it carries the meaning of the deities, after it was said "lā yamlik" according to the wording. It is also permissible for it to refer to the disbelievers, meaning: "and these [people] are not able—despite their being living, active, people of understanding—to [do] any of that, so how [could] the inanimate thing that has no sense [do it]?"

If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying ﴿and they are not able﴾ after His saying ﴿does not possess﴾? Are these not one and the same thing? I answer:

There is no returning pronoun (taqdir raji') in ﴿and they are not able﴾. Rather the meaning is: "they do not possess the power to provide," and the ability is negated of them altogether, because they are dead. Unless the returning pronoun is supposed, and the combining of the negation of possession and of ability is intended for emphasis; or it is intended: that they do not possess provision, nor is it possible for them to possess it, and that is not feasible or proper for them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 74:

﴿So do not strike forth similitudes for God.﴾ This is a figure of speech (tamthil) for associating partners with God and likening Him to His creation. [[Mahmud said: "It is a figure of speech for associating partners with God and likening Him to others... etc." Ahmad said: According to his first interpretation, the phrase lillah (for God) is connected to al-amthal (the similitudes), as if it were said: "Do not make likenesses of God and do not liken Him." According to the second interpretation, it is connected to the verb tadribu (strike forth), as if it were said: "Do not strike forth similitudes for God," for striking a similitude is only used by one who knows for one who does not know, in order to clarify to him what is hidden from him. God, exalted is He, is the All-Knowing, while you do not know. So the likening of one who does not know to One who knows is the reverse of reality. And God knows best.]] Because whoever strikes forth similitudes likens one state to another and one story to another. ﴿Indeed, God knows the true reality of what you do and its gravity﴾, and He will punish you for it with a punishment equal to its gravity, because punishment is in proportion to the magnitude of the sin. ﴿And you do not know its true reality or the true reality of His punishment﴾. It is that [ignorance] which drew you toward it and emboldened you to it. Thus this is the reason given for the prohibition of associating partners with God. It is also permissible to understand it as: "So do not strike forth similitudes for God; indeed God knows how to strike forth similitudes, and you do not know."

Then He taught them how to make a comparison, saying: "Your likeness in associating with Allah idols is like the likeness of one who equates between a slave owned, incapable of disposing of anything, and a free man who owns wealth which Allah has provided him, so that he disposes of it and spends from it as he wills."

If you ask: why did He say "a slave owned, who has no power over anything," when every slave is owned and unable to dispose of anything?

I say: As for mentioning "owned," it is to distinguish him from the free man, since the term "slave" (ʿabd) applies to both of them, as they are both servants of Allah.

As for "who has no power over anything," it is to exclude the mukatab (the slave who has contracted to buy his freedom) and the ma'dhun lahu (the slave licensed to trade), since they do have power to dispose of things.

The scholars differ on whether a slave can validly own property. The apparent and preponderant position is that he cannot.

If you ask: what is "man" (man) in His words "and one whom We have provided with a good provision from Us"? I say: Apparently it is a descriptive (mawsufa), as if it were said: "and a free man whom We have provided," to correspond with "a slave." It is not impossible that it be a relative pronoun (mawsula).

If you ask: why did He say "they are not equal" (yastawun) in the plural? I say: its meaning is:

"Are the free and the slaves equal?"

The dumb man, who was born mute, so he neither understands nor is understood, and he is a burden (kall) upon his master, meaning a weight and a dependent on the one who manages his affairs and supports him. Wherever he directs him (aynama yuwajjihhu), meaning wherever he sends him and dispatches him to pursue a need or an important matter, he brings no benefit and achieves no success. Is he equal to one who is sound in his senses, beneficial, capable of managing affairs, with right judgment and piety, who commands people to justice and goodness while he himself is upon a straight path (sirat mustaqim), following a righteous way of life and a sound religion? This is a second parable which God has struck for Himself and for what He bestows upon His servants and encompasses them with, of the effects of His mercy, His kindnesses, and His religious and worldly blessings, and for the idols, which are dead things that neither harm nor benefit.

It is also read as "ayna yatawajjahu" (wherever he turns), meaning wherever he turns, from the saying "ayna uwajjih alqa sa'daan" (wherever I direct myself, I will meet good fortune). Ibn Mas'ud read: "ayna yuwajjahu," in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 77:

﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth.﴾ That is, the knowledge of what is hidden in them from the servants, and whose knowledge is concealed from them, is exclusively His. Or he meant by the unseen of the heavens and the earth: the Day of Resurrection, on the basis that its knowledge is hidden from the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth, none of whom has been informed of it. ﴿And the matter of the Hour is not but as a glance of the eye or even nearer.﴾ That is, it is with Allah, even if it seems distant, as you say about a thing you consider near: "It is like the blink of an eye, or even nearer," when you exaggerate in considering it near.

A similar example is His saying: ﴿And they ask you to hasten the punishment, but Allah will not fail His promise. Indeed, a day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you count.﴾ That is, it is near to Him, while it is far from you. It has also been said: the meaning is that the establishing of the Hour, the causing of the living to die, and the raising of the dead, from the first and the last, will occur in the nearest and swiftest time (wa-awhaho [[His saying "wa-awhaho": that is, "and quickest." Related by al-Sihah. (Editor's note)]]). ﴿Indeed Allah is over all things competent.﴾ So He is able to establish the Hour and resurrect creation, since that is among the things within His power. Then He pointed to His power through what follows.

It has been read as أُمَّهاتِكُمْ (ummahatikum, "your mothers") with the hamza vowelled with a *damma* and also with a *kasra*. The *ha'* (ه) is an added letter in أمات (ummat), just as it is added in أراق (araqa), so that it is said أهراق (ahraqa, "he poured out"). Its addition in the singular is anomalous (shadhdh, irregular). He said:

[[My mothers are Khindif, and Ilyas is my father,
Indeed I, in the battle, am broad-chested, of high lineage, resolute in assault...]]

أمهتى خندف وإلياس أبى

Ilyas is the son of Mudar, and the Prophet's (ﷺ) ancestor is Qusayy ibn Kilab ibn Murrah.

Rakhi al-labab: broad of breast and spacious of mind. Al-labab, in origin, is the strap on the chest of the mount that prevents the saddle from slipping backward; it was applied to this by association (mujawara). Mu'tazim: resolute. Al-sawla: enduring what is disliked and plunging into it. The addition of the *ha'* in أمهة (ummah) is anomalous (shadhdh). Khindif, with a *kasra* on the *kha'* and the *dal*, was the wife of Ilyas ibn Mudar, and this was her epithet; her name was Layla. Al-khandafa is a gait like a jog. The application of "mother" and "father" to the grandmother and grandfather is a metaphor (majaz) for mere origination (mutlaq al-asala).

لا تَعْلَمُونَ شَيْئاً ﴿you know nothing﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). Its meaning is: not knowing anything of the right of the Benefactor who created you in the wombs, shaped you, formed you, and then brought you out from narrowness into ampleness.

His saying وَجَعَلَ لَكُمُ ﴿and He made for you﴾ means: He has placed in you these faculties only as instruments for removing the ignorance with which you were born, and for acquiring knowledge and acting upon it, such as thanking the Benefactor and worshipping Him, fulfilling His rights, and rising toward what will make you happy.

The plural الأفئدة (al-af'ida, "the hearts") relates to فؤاد (fu'ad) in the way الأغربة (al-aghriba, "the ravens") relates to غراب (ghurab). It is one of the paucity plurals (jumu' al-qilla, plurals of small number) which have taken the course of the plurals of abundance (jumu' al-kathra), because when only it is attested in usage, as شسوع (shusu') is attested as the plural of شسع (shis', "sandal-thong") and nothing else, the paucity form has been treated in that manner.

Qur'anic recitation variants: it is read "lam yaraw" with the ta' and with the ya' (i.e., "أَوَلَمْ يَرَوْا" read with the verb in the third-person and second-person forms, as the variant readings of the verb "yaraw"/"taraw").

"Musakhkharat" (subjected, made subservient) means made pliant for flight by means of the wings created for them and the suitable means for that [[His words "والأسباب المواتية لذلك": in al-Sihah, "ātaytuhu ʿalā dhālika al-amr mu'ātāh" means I agreed with him when I concurred with him; the common people say "wa-ātaytuhu." (ʿAynī)]].

"Al-jaww" (the atmosphere) is the air spread out from the earth in the direction of height, and "al-sakkāk" (the upper air) is farther than it [[His words "والسكاك أبعد منه": in al-Sihah, "al-sakkāk" and "al-sakkākah" are the air that meets the horizon of the sky; and also in it, "a'ʿinnat al-samāʾ" are its sheets and what stretches across its regions. And "al-ʿinān," with a fatha, is the cloud. (ʿAynī)]]. "Al-lawh" is similar to it.

What holds them up in their grasping, spreading, and standing is none but Allah, by His power.

from your houses which you inhabit, made of stone, clay, tents and other things. The sakan (dwelling) is a verbal noun used in the sense of a passive participle, meaning that to which one settles and by which one is attached, whether a house or a family. Houses (buyūtan) are the domes and structures made of leather and hides. You find them light (tastakhiffūnahā): you see them as light to carry, to strike and to dismantle and to move, on the day of your departure (ẓaʿnikum) and on the day of your residence (iqāmatikum), meaning on the day you travel, when their carrying and moving is light for you; [[Maḥmūd said: "The meaning is that their carrying and moving is light for you..." Aḥmad said: The first interpretation is preferable, because the manifestation of the favour in their lightness is realised only while travelling. As for the one who is settled, the tent is not a burden to him. How fine is al-Zamakhsharī's statement regarding "on the day of your residence":

that the intended meaning is the lightness of striking it and the ease this gives them, and God knows best.]] and on the day you alight and settle in a place where striking it has not burdened you. Or they are light for you at the times of both travel and residence, with "day" (yawm) meaning "time". And a provision (matāʿan) and a thing (shayʾan) from which you benefit (yantafiʿūna bihi) for a while (ilā ḥīn), until you finish your need of it (aṭwārakum, your journeys/needs), or until it wears out and perishes, or until you die. It is also read: yawma ẓaʿnikum, with the sukūn (silent letter pronunciation).

Of what He has created, shade from among the trees and other things that cast shade; **akناناً** (aknānan), plural of **kinn** (kinn), meaning that in which one takes shelter: houses hewn into mountains, caves and grottoes. **Sarābīl** (sarābīl), meaning shirts and garments of wool, linen, [[Mahmud said: "They are shirts and garments of wool, linen and other materials..." etc.]] Ahmad said: he means among the Arabs, and especially the cotton-dealers of the Hijaz, who are the origin of this address.]] and cotton and other materials, which protect you from the heat. He did not mention cold, because protection from heat is more important to them, and cold rarely concerns them since it is light and bearable. It was said: what protects from heat also protects from cold.

[[He continued: "It was said that what protects from heat protects from cold, so mentioning it indicates it." Ahmad said: the first view is more evident. Do you not see the precedence given to the favour of the shades that protect from the forenoon heat, in His saying, ﴿He has made for you shade from what He has created﴾? This shows that the more important matter for the addressees is protection from heat, so God bestowed upon them the greatest of His blessings in their estimation. The saying of the speaker "what protects from heat protects from cold" is witnessed against by custom, for what one is protected from heat with, the shirts, are the thin and fine ones, and that is not the means of protection against cold. Indeed, if a person wore in each of the two seasons, summer and winter, the other's clothing, he would be considered a fool.]] Thus the mention of heat indicates cold.

**Sarābīl** (sarābīl) that protect you from your violence: he means coats of mail and body armour. The word **sarbāl** applies generally to anything made of iron or other material.

﴿So that you may submit﴾: that is, that you may reflect upon His abundant blessings, and so believe in Him and submit to Him. It is also read **tuslimūn** (tuslimūn), from safety, meaning: that you may give thanks and so be safe from punishment. Or: that your hearts may be safe from polytheism. It was said: that you may be safe from wounds by wearing armour.

If they turn away, [and] do not accept from you, then your excuse has been established, since you have already delivered what was incumbent upon you of conveying [the message]. He mentioned the cause of the excuse, which is the delivery, in order to indicate the effect.

﴿They recognize the blessing of God﴾, which We have enumerated, inasmuch as they acknowledge it and that it is from God; ﴿then they deny it﴾ by worshipping other than the One who bestowed it, and by their saying: "It is from God, but it is by the intercession of our gods." It was also said: their denial is their saying, "We inherited it from our fathers." And it was said: it is their saying, "Were it not for so-and-so, I would not have obtained such-and-such," concerning some of the blessings of God. Such speech is not permissible when one does not believe that it is from God, and that He caused it to flow through the hand of so-and-so and made him a means of attaining it.

﴿And most of them are the disbelievers﴾, i.e., the deniers, those who do not acknowledge [it]. It was also said: ﴿the blessing of God﴾ is the prophethood of Muhammad, peace be upon him. They used to recognize it, then deny it out of obstinacy, and "most of them" are the deniers who reject it in their hearts.

If you ask: what is the meaning of "then" (thumma)? I say: it indicates that their denial is something strange after the recognition has occurred, because the proper course for one who recognizes a blessing is to acknowledge it, not to deny it.

Shahidan (a witness): their prophet will bear witness for them and against them, to their faith and assent, and to their disbelief and denial. Then, "those who disbelieved will not be permitted [to offer excuses]." The meaning: they have no proof. Their not being given leave indicates that they have neither proof nor excuse. Likewise, it is related from al-Hasan: "nor will they be asked to make amends," i.e., nor will they be asked to seek the pleasure [of their Lord]. It will not be said to them, "Seek the pleasure of your Lord," because the Hereafter is not an abode of action.

If you ask, "What is the meaning of this 'thumma' (then)?" I say: its meaning is that they are tried (yamunnūn) [[The word "yamunnūn" in al-Sihah: manaituhu and minituhu mean I tested him (ibtalaytuhu). (ʿ)]] after the testimony of the prophets with something more grievous than it, namely that they are prevented from speaking, so they are not permitted to put forward an excuse or to present a proof. The accusative of "the day" is governed by an implied verb, its estimated form being: "Remember the day when We raise up [a witness from every nation]," or "the day We raise up... they fell into what they fell into." Likewise, when they see the punishment, it will surprise them and weigh heavily upon them: "so it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved," like His saying: "Rather, it will come upon them suddenly, and it will confound them..." (Qur'an 21:40), and so on.

If they mean by "their partners" their gods, then the meaning of "our partners" is our gods whom we used to call partners. If they mean the devils, then it is because they are their partners in disbelief and their companions in error. And "we call upon" means "we worship."

If you say: why did they say "indeed, you are liars," when they were in fact worshipping them in truth? I say: since they were not pleased with their worship, their worship was as if it were not worship. The proof of this is the statement of the angels, "They used to worship the jinn" (34:41), meaning that the jinn were pleased with their worship, not us, so they were the ones worshipped instead of us. Or they denied them in calling them partners and gods, glorifying God above having any partner.

And if "the partners" is meant as the devils, it is permissible that they be "liars" in their saying "indeed, you are liars," just as the Devil says: "Indeed, I disown what you associated with me before" (14:22). "And they will throw down" means those who did wrong. "Throwing down the peace" means submitting to God's command and judgment after refusal and arrogance in this world. "And what they used to invent" (yaftaruna) was lost to them, that is, what they had fabricated, namely that God has partners and that these would help them and intercede for them, has vanished from them when they denied them and disowned them.

Those who disbelieved within themselves and led others to disbelief: God will multiply their punishment, just as they multiplied their disbelief. It was said concerning the increase of their punishment: there are snakes like the Bukht (Bactrian camels) and scorpions like mules, and when one of them stings, its victim feels its venom (ḥumma) for forty autumns. [[His saying "ḥummatuhā" (its venom) is ḥummat al-ʿaqrab, with the lightened pronunciation, and the hāʾ is a substitute for the lām, and it is its poison. As for ḥummat al-ḥarr (the heat of the sun), it is pronounced with emphasis, and it is its most intense part, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] It was also said: they will be brought out of the Fire to the Zamhareer (the bitter cold), and from the intensity of its cold they will hasten back to the Fire. ﴿بِمَا كَانُوا يُفْسِدُونَ﴾ (for what they used to corrupt): by their being corruptors of people, by barring them from the way of God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 89:

﴿A witness against them from among themselves﴾: that is, their Prophet, because he used to raise up prophets for the nations from among them. ﴿And We have sent down to you, [O Muhammad], the Book as an explanation of all things﴾ — [O Muhammad], a witness over these, over your community. ﴿Tibyan﴾: a clear, eloquent explanation. Its pattern is like "tilqa'" (in the sense of "in front of"), with the first letter vowelled with a kasra. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) permitted its first letter to be vowelled with a fatha outside the Qur'an.

If it is said: how was the Qur'an an explanation of all things?

I say: the meaning is that it makes clear every matter of the religion, since it contained explicit statements on some of them and referral to the Sunnah (the Prophetic tradition) on others, where it commanded following the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and obeying him. It was also said: ﴿and he does not speak from [his own] desire﴾. And it exhorts toward consensus (ijma', scholarly agreement) in His words: ﴿and follows a path other than that of the believers﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) approved for his community the following of his Companions and emulating their footsteps, in his saying (ﷺ): "My Companions are like the stars; whichever of them you follow, you will be guided." [[Narrated by al-Daraqutni in al-Mu'talif from the narration of Salam ibn Salim from al-Harith ibn Ghusn from al-A'mash from Abu Sufyan from Jabir, raised (to the Prophet). Salam is weak. It was also narrated in Gharib Malik by way of Humayd ibn Zayd from Malik from Ja'far ibn Muhammad from his father from Jabir, in the course of a hadith, in which is: "So whichever saying of my Companions you take, you will be guided; the likeness of my Companions is only that of the star: whoever takes by one of them is guided." And he said: it is not established from Malik; and its narrators below Malik are unknown. It was also narrated by Abd ibn Humayd and al-Daraqutni in al-Fada'il from the hadith of Hamza al-Harirí from Nafi' from Ibn Umar. They accused Hamza of fabrication. It was narrated by al-Qada'i in Musnad al-Shihab from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, and in it is Ja'far ibn Abd al-Wahid al-Hashimi, whom they declared a liar. It was narrated by Ibn Tahir from the narration of Bishr ibn al-Husayn from al-Zubayr ibn Adi from Anas. Bishr was also accused. It was narrated by al-Bayhaqi in al-Madkhal from the narration of Juwaybir from al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and Juwaybir is abandoned. And from the narration of Juwaybir also from Hawwab ibn Abd Allah, raised, and it is mursal (with a missing companion). Al-Bayhaqi said: this text is well known, but all its chains are weak. He also narrated in al-Madkhal from Umar, raised: "I asked my Lord about what my Companions disagree on after me. So it was revealed to me: O Muhammad, your Companions with Me are like the stars in the sky, some brighter than others; whoever takes by any of what they hold in their disagreement, he is upon guidance with Me." In its chain is Abd al-Rahim ibn Zayd al-Sahmi, who is abandoned.]] They exerted effort, analogized, and paved the paths of analogy and independent reasoning (ijtihad). Thus the Sunnah, consensus, analogy and independent reasoning all rest upon the explanation of the Book, and for this reason it was an explanation of all things.

The obligatory is justice (ʿadl). Al-Zamakhsharī said: "*Al-ʿadl* means the obligatory, and *al-iḥsān* means the recommended." Ahmad said: Bringing the two together under one command indicates the view of those who say that the imperative form, namely this one formed from the hamza, the mīm and the rāʾ (*amr*, not the form *afʿal*), applies to both categories by way of shared meaning (*tawāṭuʾ*), its locus being the common element between them, which is the demand. And Allah knows best.

Because Allah, exalted is He, is just toward His servants in it. Al-Zamakhsharī resumed: "The obligatory was only justice because Allah, exalted is He, is just toward His servants in it..." etc. Ahmad said: This is an entrance into Muʿtazilism. The doctrine of the Muʿtazilah (the rationalist school that held Allah is bound by justice as humans understand it) is that imposing what cannot be borne is impossible, because it is injustice and tyranny, and that is impossible for Allah.

The truth and the Sunnah hold that every decree of Allah is just, that imposing what cannot be borne is permissible for Him and is a form of justice from Him: "He cannot be questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned." Rather, all obligations are, in fact, beyond capacity (*istiṭāʿah*, power to act), in accordance with the monotheism (*tawḥīd*) of the People of the Sunnah (*Ahl al-Sunnah*), who hold that everything that exists came into being and was brought into existence by the power of Allah, exalted is He, with no partner in His dominion. How could a partner be a servant subjected in the grip of His sovereignty? This is pure monotheism.

If the servant is obligated to do what is itself the act of Allah, then this is precisely the imposition of what cannot be borne. Yet that is justice from Allah, exalted is He, and His conclusive proof stands against the one obligated, by what He created in him of ability and facility in voluntary acts, which are the loci of obligations.

So He made what He imposed upon them fall within their capacity. "And beneficence" is the recommended. He attached His command to both together, because the obligation cannot avoid some shortfall, which the recommended act makes good.

Al-Zamakhsharī resumed: "He combined them in the command because the obligation is never free of defect and shortfall, which the recommended act compensates for..." etc. Ahmad said: This is a fine point by which one answers the question of someone who asks why the Prophet (ﷺ) ruled that a man attains success while abandoning the Sunnahs. It is said: the one ruled successful for it is only the one who is truthful, in that his obligatory acts are free from defect of deficiency or excess. And Allah knows best.

So it is compensated by the recommended act. For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, to the man who had taught him the obligations and then said, "By Allah, I will add nothing to them and reduce nothing from them": "He will succeed if he is truthful." (Agreed upon, from the narration of Ṭalḥah ibn ʿUbayd Allāh, one of the Ten (promised Paradise), may Allah be pleased with them.) Thus he tied success to the condition of truthfulness and freedom from shortfall.

He (ﷺ) also said: "Be steadfast, and you will not be able to count (your good deeds)." (Narrated by Ibn Mājah, al-Ḥākim, Aḥmad, Ibn Abī Shaybah, al-Dārimī and Abū Yaʿlā, from the narration of Sālim ibn Abī al-Jaʿd from Thawbān. It is *munqaṭiʿ* (broken in its chain). Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ṭabarānī narrated it through another route from Thawbān. Al-Ḥākim narrated it from the narration of al-Aʿmash from Abū Sufyān from Jābir. al-Ṭabarānī and al-ʿUqaylī narrated it from the hadith of Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, and in it is al-Wāqidī. Ibn Abī Shaybah, Isḥāq, al-Bazzār and al-Ṭabarānī narrated it from Layth ibn Abī Sulaym from Mujāhid from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, and Layth is weak. al-Bazzār indicated that he alone narrated it.)

So one should not abandon, among the supererogatory acts, what makes up for the shortfall in obligations. "Obscenities" are what exceed the limits set by Allah. "The unjust" is what reason rejects. Ahmad said: This is also a hint toward Muʿtazilism. Had he said "the unjust is what the Law (*shariʿah*) rejects," it would have been in accord with the truth, but he does not abandon the innovation of the Muʿtazilah regarding the goodness and ugliness of things by reason (*taḥsīn wa-taqbīḥ*). And Allah is the Granter of success.

"Transgression" is seeking to exceed bounds through injustice. Al-Zamakhsharī resumed: "Transgression is seeking to exceed bounds through injustice..." Ahmad said: Its original meaning is seeking, as in *ibtighāʾ wajh Allāh* (seeking the face of Allah) and *ibtighāʾ marḍāt Allāh* (seeking the pleasure of Allah). But by common usage its unrestricted form has become specific to seeking injustice.

When the cursing of the accursed against the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah ennoble his face, was removed from the sermons... Al-Zamakhsharī resumed: "And when the cursing of the accursed against the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah ennoble his face, was removed from the sermons..." etc. Ahmad said: Perhaps this verse was set in place of that fault. Observe the correspondence between the mention of the prohibition of transgression in it and the hadith that is reported, that whoever opposes ʿAlī is a transgressor, where the Prophet (ﷺ) said to ʿAmmār, who was of ʿAlī's party: "The transgressing group will kill you." And Allah knows best. Then he was killed alongside ʿAlī at the Battle of Ṣiffīn.

Was the cursing of the accursed against the Commander of the Faithful ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, an established practice? This verse was placed in its position. By my life, it was indeed an obscenity, an unjust act and a transgression. Allah multiplied for the one who initiated it wrath, punishment and disgrace, in answer to the supplication of His Prophet: "And whoever opposes him (ʿāda man ʿādāh)."

This is part of the hadith of Ghadīr Khumm concerning the virtue of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him. It was narrated by al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Ḥibbān and al-Ḥākim from the narration of al-Aʿmash from Ḥabīb ibn Abī Thābit from al-Ṭufayl from Zayd ibn Arqam, and in it is this wording.

al-Nasāʾī also narrated it from the narration of Sharīk: I said to Abū Isḥāq: "Did you hear al-Barāʾ narrate from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: On the day of Ghadīr Khumm, [he said] "Whoever I am his master (mawlā), then ʿAlī is his master. O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and oppose whoever opposes him." He said: "Yes." It was also narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah, Abū Yaʿlā and al-Bazzār through another route from Sharīk, from Idrīs ibn Yazīd al-Awdī, from his father, from Abū Hurayrah, and ʿIkrimah ibn Ibrāhīm followed him from Idrīs in al-Ṭabarānī's narration. al-Ṭabarī also narrated it through the route of Sulaymān ibn Qawm from Abū Isḥāq from Ḥabashī ibn Junādah. al-Nasāʾī also narrated it through the route of Muhājir ibn Mismār from ʿĀ'ishah bint Saʿd from her father, that the Prophet (ﷺ) "took ʿAlī's hand on the day of Ghadīr Khumm and said: Whoever I am his guardian (walī), this one is his guardian. O Allah, befriend whoever befriends him and oppose whoever opposes him." al-Ḥākim narrated it from the narration of Muslim al-Mulāʾī from Ḥathmah ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Saʿd ibn Mālik, similarly. On the subject there is also a narration from Ibn ʿUmar, which al-Ṭabarānī narrated through ʿAṭiyyah from him, and al-Bazzār through Jamīl ibn ʿUmārah from Sālim from his father. And from Anas and others, al-Ṭabarānī in *al-Ṣaghīr* narrated it through the narration of Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif from ʿUmayrah ibn Saʿd, who said: "I witnessed ʿAlī on the pulpit appealing to the Companions: Who heard him say on the day of Ghadīr Khumm what he said? Twelve men stood up, among them Abū Hurayrah, Abū Saʿīd and Anas." And from Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī narrated it at length. And from Ṭalḥah, al-Ḥākim narrated it through the narration of Rifāʿah ibn Iyās al-ʿAmmī from his father from his grandfather, who said: "We were with ʿAlī on the day of the Camel, and he sent to Ṭalḥah and said to him: I adjure you by Allah, did you not hear the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say such-and-such?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Then why do you fight me?" He said: "I did not remember," and Ṭalḥah withdrew. And from Jābir, Abū Yaʿlā and al-Ṭabarānī in *Musnad al-Shāmiyyīn* narrated it through Ibn Lahīʿah from Bakr ibn Sawādah from Qabīṣah ibn Dhuʾayb and Abū Salamah from Jābir. And from Ḥudhayfah ibn Usayd, al-Ṭabarānī narrated it. Ibn ʿUqdah compiled the portion of the hadith of Ghadīr Khumm, narrating it through a group of other Companions besides these: among them ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir, al-ʿAbbās and his son, al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī and al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿAlī, ʿAbd Allāh ibn Jaʿfar, Salmān al-Fārisī, Samurah ibn Jundab, Salamah ibn al-Akwaʿ, Zayd ibn Ḥārithah, Abū Rāfiʿ, Zayd ibn Thābit al-Anṣārī, Yaʿlā ibn Murrah, and others.

It was the cause of the conversion to Islam of ʿUthmān ibn Maẓʿūn.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verses 91–92:

"The covenant of Allah": it is the pledge of allegiance (bay'ah) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) upon Islam. ﴿Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you, they are only pledging allegiance to Allah.﴾ ﴿And do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾, i.e., after their confirmation by the name of Allah. Akkada and wakkada are two eloquent forms (lughatan fasihatan), and the original root is waw, with the hamzah as a substitute. ﴿Surety﴾ means witness and guardian, because the surety (kafil) observes the state of the one he stands surety for and is watchful over him. ﴿And do not be like her who unravels her spinning after it has been made strong, breaking it into pieces﴾: ankath is the plural of nakth, which is what is unwound of a twist. It is said: she was Rayta bint Sa'd ibn Taym, and she was a khar'a (foolish woman). She acquired a spindle the length of a forearm, a small hook like a finger, and a large whorl appropriate to its size. She and her maidservants would spin from morning until noon, and then she would order them and they would unravel what they had spun. ﴿Taking them as a deceit⦂ (takhidhun) is a circumstantial clause (hal) and dakhalan is one of the two objects of "ittakhadha" (to take). The meaning: do not break your oaths, making them a means of deceit (dakhal) among you, i.e., corruption and treachery [[The saying "wadaghalan" in al-Sihah: "al-daghal" with a fatha on the gh: corruption, like "al-dakhal" (ʿ)]], ﴿because one community is more numerous than another community﴾, meaning the group of Quraysh, who are greater in number and more abundant in wealth than a community of the believers. ﴿Indeed, Allah only tests you by it﴾: the pronoun refers to "that one community be", since it carries the sense of a verbal noun; i.e., He tests you by their being more numerous, to see whether you cling to the means of fulfilling the covenant of Allah and what you have pledged upon yourselves and confirmed of oaths of allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), or whether you are deceived by the multitude of Quraysh, their wealth and their strength, and the fewness and poverty and weakness of the believers. ﴿And He will surely make clear to you﴾: this is a warning and admonition against opposing the religion of Islam.

﴿Had God willed, He would have made you one community﴾ (ḥanīfah muslimah), submitting by way of compulsion and constraint. [Mahmud said: "Its meaning is by way of compulsion and coercion."] Ahmad said: This is a Mu'tazili interpretation (the Mu'tazila being a rationalist theological school), and he had already put forward similar interpretations in the sister verses of this one. His aim is to escape the truth derived from the conditioning of the will with *law* (lau, "if"), which indicates that God's will for the faith of all of creation did not take place, and that He willed from them only division and difference: some believe and some disbelieve, some affirm and some deny, as has happened among them. Had He willed to include them all in faith, it would have occurred. Thus al-Zamakhshari contradicts this text and says: He did will to make them one community, ḥanīfah muslimah, but His intention did not come to pass. If he is asked, "To what, then, is the will in the verse to be applied?" he says: to the will that they have faith by compulsion, not by choice; and this will did not, by consensus, take place.

[And He is able to do that, but wisdom required that He lead astray whomever He wills, which is to forsake whoever He knows chooses disbelief (kufr) and persists in it, and guide whomever He wills, which is to show kindness to whoever He knows chooses faith.]

[Note: His words "which is to forsake whoever He knows chooses disbelief" are the view of the Mu'tazila. As for Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni tradition), misguidance (iḍlāl) is the creation of error in the heart, because according to them it is permissible for God to create evil, unlike the Mu'tazila, as is explained in its proper place. (ʿ)]

That is: He based the matter on choice and on what merits kindness or forsaking, reward and punishment, and did not base it on compulsion (ijbār), by which none of these would be merited. He confirmed this with His words ﴿But you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾, and had He been the one who compels to misguidance and guidance, He would not have established for them an action about which they are questioned.

[Resuming his words. Mahmud said: Among what indicates that God did not base the matter on compulsion but on choice is the Exalted's words ﴿But you will surely be questioned about what you used to do﴾. Had He been the one who compels to guidance and misguidance, He would not have established for them what they are questioned about.]

Ahmad said: As for the Ahl al-Sunna, whom the author calls *Mujbirah* (Jabriyya, those who affirm compulsion), they are far removed from compulsion, because they affirm for the servant capability, choice and acts. Along with that, they affirm God's unity in its true sense, making God's power the one that brings things into existence and is the effective cause, while the servant's power is merely concomitant. This is to distinguish between the voluntary and the coerced, and by it God's proof is established against His servant. And God is the Granter of success.

Then he repeated the prohibition against taking oaths as a means of deceit among themselves, as an emphasis upon them and a demonstration of the gravity of what such oaths lead to: "lest a foot slip after it was firmly planted," that is, lest your feet slip away from the highway of Islam after they had been firmly set upon it. "And you taste evil in this world," through your turning away from the way of Allah and your departure from the religion. Or [it means] through your turning others away, because if they broke the oaths of allegiance and apostatized, they would make the breaking of them a precedent for others to follow. "And for you is a great punishment in the Hereafter."

This was a group of people who had embraced Islam in Mecca. Satan made their outrage at what they saw of the Quraysh's dominance, their oppression of the Muslims, and the harm inflicted on them seem appealing to them, and [he made appealing to them] the promises that the Quraysh were making to them if they returned [to disbelief]: that they would break the pledge they had given to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So Allah made them steadfast.

﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾: do not substitute the covenant of Allah and the pledge to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for a small price, a fleeting, trivial gain from this world, which is what the Quraysh were promising and dangling before them if they returned.

﴿What is with Allah is better for you﴾: what is with Allah, namely your victory and the spoils you will gain [in this world], and the reward of the Hereafter, is better for you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 96:

What is with you of the goods of this world will come to an end, and what is with Allah of the treasures of His mercy is lasting and will never end.

It is also read as "lanajziyanna" (with the nun) and as "layajziyanna" (with the ya'), [meaning:] "Those who were patient" (alladhina sabaru) over the harm of the polytheists and the hardships of Islam.

If you ask: why was "qadam" (foot) made singular and indefinite? [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "If you ask why 'qadam' was made singular and indefinite..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Among the functions of indefiniteness here is the expression of paucity, as in His words, "and an attentive ear will retain it" (wa-ta'iyaha udhunun wa'iyah), and in His words, "Fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has sent forward for tomorrow" (ittaqu Allaha wa-lanzur nafsun ma qaddamat li-ghad). So He made "udhun" (ear) and "nafs" (soul) indefinite, indicating fewness of those who listen and retain what is decreed for their rectitude, and fewness of those among creation who look to the matter of their return. And Allah is the Granter of success.]

I say: it is to magnify the matter that a single foot should slip from the path of truth after having been firmly set upon it, so how much more so many feet?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 97:

If you ask: "Man" (man) in itself applies to both males and females, so what is the purpose of specifying them with "male or female"? I answer: it is an indefinite term which, unrestrictedly, is suitable for both kinds; however, when it is mentioned, the apparent reference is to males. So it is said "from a male or a female," for specification, so that the promise encompasses both kinds together. "A good life" (hayat tayyibah) means, in this world, and this is the apparent meaning, due to His saying "and We will surely reward them" (wa-la-najziyannahum), meaning God promised them the reward of this world and the Hereafter, like His saying "So God gave them the reward of this world and the good reward of the Hereafter" (fa-atahumu Allahu thawab al-dunya wa-husn thawab al-akhirah). That is because the believer who does righteous deeds, whether wealthy or poor, lives a good life if he is wealthy, so there is no dispute about it. If he is poor, what makes his life good is with him, namely contentment and satisfaction with God's apportionment. As for the wicked person, his situation is the reverse: if he is poor, there is no difficulty regarding his state, but if he is wealthy, greed does not let him enjoy his life. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "A good life: lawful provision (al-rizq al-halal)."

It is related from al-Hasan: "Contentment (al-qana'ah)." It is related from Qatadah: "Meaning, in Paradise." It was also said: it is the sweetness of obedience and success placed in his heart.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verses 98–100:

When He mentioned righteous deeds and promised reward for them, He followed this with His saying, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾, signalling that seeking refuge (isti'adhah) is among the righteous deeds for which Allah bestows abundant reward. The meaning is: when you intend to recite the Qur'an, then seek refuge, like His saying, ﴿When you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾, and like your saying: "When you eat, say the name of Allah." If you ask: why is the intention to perform an action expressed with the wording of the action itself? I answer: because the action comes into being at the moment of intention and resolve without any separation and in accordance with it, so it is connected to it by a strong cause and a manifest association.

And on the authority of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "I recited before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and I said: 'A'udhu bis-Sami' al-'Alim min ash-shaytan ar-rajim (I seek refuge in the All-Hearing, All-Knowing from the accursed Satan).' He said to me: 'O son of Umm 'Abd, say: A'udhu billah min ash-shaytan ar-rajim (I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan). Thus Jibril (peace be upon him) recited it to me from the Pen, from the Preserved Tablet.'" [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi with an unbroken chain (musalsal) through his teacher Abu al-Fadl Muhammad ibn Ja'far al-Khuza'i to Ibn Mas'ud. Al-Wahidi also narrated it in al-Wasit from al-Tha'labi.]]

﴿He has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾, that is, he has no dominion or sway over the friends of Allah, meaning: they do not accept from him nor obey him in what he desires from them of following his steps. ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and who associate partners with Him (bihi mushrikun)﴾. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to their Lord. It is also permissible for it to refer to Satan, in the sense of: because of him, by his deception and his whispering.

﴿He has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord﴾, that is, he has no dominion or sway over the friends of Allah, meaning: they do not accept from him nor obey him in what he desires from them of following his steps. ﴿His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and who associate partners with Him (bihi mushrikun)﴾. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 101:

"Replacing a verse with another verse" means naskh (abrogation). God, exalted is He, abrogates laws with laws, because they are benefits (maslahah, public good), and what was a benefit yesterday may be a harm today, and its opposite is a benefit. God, exalted is He, knows benefits and harms, so He establishes what He wills and abrogates what He wills by His wisdom. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And God knows best what He sends down﴾ ﴿They say, "You are only a fabricator."﴾ They found an opening for criticism, so they criticized, and that was due to their ignorance and their distance from knowledge of the abrogating and the abrogated (al-nasikh wa'l-mansukh). They used to say: "Muhammad mocks his companions: he orders them today to do something and forbids them from it tomorrow, bringing them what is easier." But they lied, for he abrogated the harder with the easier, the easier with the harder, the easier with the easier, and the harder with the harder, because the aim is benefit, not humiliation or hardship.

If you say: Does the mention of replacing a verse with a verse indicate that the Qur'an is abrogated only by its like, and that it is not valid to abrogate it by other than it, such as the Sunnah, consensus (ijma') or analogy (qiyas)?

I say: It indicates that a Qur'an verse may be abrogated by its like, and it does not negate its being abrogated by other than it. Moreover, the clear, widely transmitted Sunnah is equal to the Qur'an in obligating knowledge, so abrogating it by that is like abrogating it by its like. As for consensus, analogy, and a Sunnah whose authenticity is not certain, it is not valid to abrogate the Qur'an by them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 102:

In "yunazzilu" and "nazzalahu" and what is in them of revelation (tanzil) little by little, according to the occurrences and the considerations (maslahah): an indication that substitution (tabdil) is by way of considerations, like revelation (tanzil), and that leaving abrogation (naskh) is in the position of sending it down all at once, in that it departs from wisdom (hikmah).

"Ruh al-Qudus" (the Holy Spirit) is Jibril, peace be upon him. It is attributed to "al-Quds," which is purity, as one says:

"Hatim al-Jud" (Hatim of generosity) and "Zayd al-Khayr" (Zayd of goodness). The intended meaning is "al-ruh al-muqaddas" (the sanctified spirit), and "Hatim al-Jawad" (Hatim the generous), and "Zayd al-Khayr" (Zayd the good). And "al-muqaddas" means purified from sins. It has been read with a damma on the dal and with a sukun (silent dal). 

"Bil-haqq" (with the truth) is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal), meaning: He sent it down while it was joined with wisdom. That is, abrogation is among the truth, "liyuthabbita alladhina amanu" (to make firm those who believe), by testing them with abrogation, until when they say about it, "It is the truth from our Lord and the wisdom," He rules for them with firmness of footing, soundness of certainty, and tranquility of hearts, since Allah is Wise, so He does not do except what is wisdom and right. "Hudan wa bushra" (guidance and good news) are objects of purpose (maf'ul lahu), coordinated with the place of "liyuthabbita." The estimate is: as firmness for them, and guidance, and good tidings. In this there is an indirect allusion to the occurrence of the opposites of these qualities for others. It has been read "liyuthabbit" with the lightened form.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verse 103:

They meant by "the human being" a slave of Huwaytib ibn ʿAbd al-ʿUzzaa, who had embraced Islam and whose Islam was good; his name was ʿĀʾish or Yaʿīsh, and he was a man of books. It is also said that he was Jabr, a Roman slave belonging to ʿĀmir ibn al-Ḥaḍramī. It is also said that they were two slaves, Jabr and Yasār, who used to make swords in Mecca and recite the Torah and the Gospel. The Messenger of God (ﷺ), whenever he passed by, would stop by them and listen to what they recited. So they said, "They are teaching him." This was said to one of them, and he replied, "Rather, he is teaching me."

It is also said that it was Salmān al-Fārisī.

"Al-lisān" means language. It is said: "alḥada al-qabr" and "laḥada," and he is "mulḥid" and "maljūd," when he makes the digging of the grave deviate from straightness; he digs in one side of it. Then it was used figuratively for every deviation from straightness, and they say: "Fulān alḥada fī qawlihi" (so-and-so deviated in his statement), and "alḥada fī dīnihi" (he deviated in his religion). From this comes "al-mulḥid" (the heretic), because he has turned his doctrine away from all religions, not turning it from one religion to another.

The meaning: the tongue of the man towards whom they incline their speech from straightness is a foreign (aʿjamī) tongue, unclear; "and this is the Qur'an, a clear Arabic tongue" (lisānun ʿarabiyyun mubīn), possessing eloquence and clarity, rejecting their saying and nullifying their slander. It was also read as "yulḥidūna" with a fatḥa on the yāʾ and the ḥāʾ. In the reading of al-Ḥasan: "al-lisāna alladhī yulḥidūna ilayhi" with the definite article on "lisān."

If you say: What is the place (i'rab) of the clause "lisānu alladhī yulḥidūna ilayhi aʿjamiyyun"? I say: it has no place in the sentence, because it is a resumptive (mustaʾnafa) response to their saying. Similar to it is His saying: "Allāhu aʿlamu ḥaythu yajʿalu risālatah" (God knows best where to place His message), after His saying: "wa-idhā jāʾat-hum āyatun qālū lan nuʾmina ḥattā nuʾtā mithla mā ūtiya rusulu Allāh" ("And when a sign comes to them they say: We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God").

The meaning is: fabricating lies befits only one who does not believe, because he does not expect any punishment for it. ﴿And those—﴾ a reference to the Quraysh—﴿they are the liars﴾. That is, they are the ones who do not believe, and so they are the liars. Or it refers to those who do not believe: that is, they are the liars in the true and complete sense, perfect in lying, because denying the signs of Allah is the greatest of lies. Or: they are those whose habit is lying, who do not care about it in anything, and whom neither manliness (muruwwah) nor religion restrains from it. Or: they are the liars in their saying, ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verses 106–109:

﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief﴾ is a substitute (badal, apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, on the view that ﴿and they are the liars﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) between the substitute and what it substitutes for. The meaning is: only those who disbelieve in God after having believed fabricate lies.

He excepted from them the one who is compelled, so he does not fall under the ruling of fabrication. Then he said: ﴿except for one whose breast is open to disbelief﴾, meaning one who is content with it in his soul and holds it as his belief, ﴿upon them is wrath from God﴾. It is also permissible that it be a substitute for the subject (mubtada') which is ﴿they﴾, with the sense: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, they are the liars.﴾ Or it may be a substitute for the predicate (khabar) which is ﴿the liars﴾, with the sense: ﴿and they are those who disbelieve in God after their belief.﴾ It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as a censure (dham). Some have allowed that ﴿whoever disbelieves in God﴾ be a conditional subject (shart mubtada'), with its response omitted, because the response of ﴿whoever opens his breast﴾ indicates it, as if it were said: whoever disbelieves in God, upon them is wrath, except the one who is compelled; but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath.

It is narrated that some people of Mecca were tested and apostatized from Islam after entering it. Among them was one who was compelled, so he uttered the word of disbelief with his tongue while believing in faith. Among them were ʿAmmar, his parents Yasir and Sumayya, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab, and Salim. They were tortured. As for Sumayya, she was tied between two camels, and a spear was thrust into her private parts, and they said: "You became Muslim for the sake of men." So she was killed. Yasir was killed too, and they were the first two to be killed in Islam. As for ʿAmmar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue, under compulsion. It was said: "O Messenger of God, ʿAmmar has disbelieved." He said: "No. Indeed ʿAmmar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then ʿAmmar came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) weeping, and the Prophet (ﷺ) began to wipe his eyes and said: "What is the matter with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said."

Among them was Jabr, the freedman of al-Hadrami, whom his master compelled, so he disbelieved; then his master and he became Muslim, their Islam was good, and they emigrated. [[This was related by al-Tha'labi from Ibn ʿAbbas without a chain. al-Hakim related from the hadith of Zirr from Ibn Masʿud, who said: "The first to openly display their Islam were seven," and he mentioned them until he said: "The polytheists seized them and dressed them in iron armour..." – the hadith. He repeated this to him three times, and he repeated his answer, so he killed him. When this reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he said: "As for the first, he took the concession of God. As for the second, he proclaimed the truth, so good tidings to him."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related it in his Tafsir from Maʿmar, who said: "I heard that Musaylima seized two men," and he mentioned it in similar words. al-Wahidi mentioned in al-Maghazi that the name of the one killed was Habib ibn Zayd, uncle of ʿAbbad ibn Tamim, and the name of the other was ʿAbd Allah ibn Wahb al-Aslami. ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief﴾ is a substitute (badal, apposition) for ﴿those who do not believe in the signs of God﴾, on the view that ﴿and they are the liars﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraD) between the substitute and what it substitutes for. The meaning is: only those who disbelieve in God after having believed fabricate lies.

He excepted from them the one who is compelled, so he does not fall under the ruling of fabrication. Then he said: ﴿except for one whose breast is open to disbelief﴾, meaning one who is content with it in his soul and holds it as his belief, ﴿upon them is wrath from God﴾. It is also permissible that it be a substitute for the subject (mubtada') which is ﴿they﴾, with the sense: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in God after his belief, they are the liars.﴾ Or it may be a substitute for the predicate (khabar) which is ﴿the liars﴾, with the sense: ﴿and they are those who disbelieve in God after their belief.﴾ It is also permissible that it be in the accusative as a censure (dham). Some have allowed that ﴿whoever disbelieves in God﴾ be a conditional subject (shart mubtada'), with its response omitted, because the response of ﴿whoever opens his breast﴾ indicates it, as if it were said: whoever disbelieves in God, upon them is wrath, except the one who is compelled; but whoever opens his breast to disbelief, upon them is wrath.

It is narrated that some people of Mecca were tested and apostatized from Islam after entering it. Among them was one who was compelled, so he uttered the word of disbelief with his tongue while believing in faith. Among them were ʿAmmar, his parents Yasir and Sumayya, Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab, and Salim. They were tortured. As for Sumayya, she was tied between two camels, and a spear was thrust into her private parts, and they said: "You became Muslim for the sake of men." So she was killed. Yasir was killed too, and they were the first two to be killed in Islam. As for ʿAmmar, he gave them what they wanted with his tongue, under compulsion. It was said: "O Messenger of God, ʿAmmar has disbelieved." He said: "No. Indeed ʿAmmar is filled with faith from his head to his feet, and faith has mingled with his flesh and blood." Then ʿAmmar came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) weeping, and the Prophet (ﷺ) began to wipe his eyes and said: "What is the matter with you? If they return to you, then return to them with what you said."

Among them was Jabr, the freedman of al-Hadrami, whom his master compelled, so he disbelieved; then his master and he became Muslim, their Islam was good, and they emigrated. God struck a parable: a town (qaryah) that was secure and tranquil, its provision coming to it abundantly from every place. That is, He made the town whose condition this was an example for every people upon whom Allah bestowed favours, and the favour made them insolent, so they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah sent down upon them His vengeance. It is permissible that a town of this description be intended as a hypothetical one, and that there was among the towns of the earlier peoples a town whose condition was this, and Allah made it a parable for Makkah, as a warning lest it suffer a similar end. Al-an'um is the plural of ni'mah, dropping the consideration of the ta' (as in dir', plural adri'), or it is the plural of ni'am, like bu's and ab'us.

If you say: "idhaqah" (making to taste) and "libas" (garment) are metaphors; what is the justification for their validity? And the metaphorical "idhaqah" is applied to the metaphorical "libas"; what is the justification for applying it to it? [[Mahmud said: "If you say, 'idhaqah and libas are metaphors, what is the justification for applying idhaqah to libas...?"]]

Ahmad says: This section of his speech deserves that the scholars of rhetoric write it with molten gold rather than ink. He considered both of them together in the words of the Exalted: "Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, so their commerce has not profited them, nor were they guided" (2:16). Here "buying" is used metaphorically for their choosing error over guidance, though they were able to choose guidance over it. Then he attended to the metaphorical buying with His words "so their commerce has not profited them," using "commerce" and "profit" to suit the metaphor of buying. Then he attended to the original literal meaning for which the metaphor was used with His words "nor were they guided," for it is free of metaphor; for if it were said, "Those are the ones who went astray, and were not guided," the statement would be literal, stripped of the garment of metaphor. Attending to the borrowed term in its own domain is like the tarshih (nurturing) of a metaphor in its own domain. From this is the verse:

When the devil gaped at her nape... we pulled him out with a twisted rope.

Here he made the devil gaping at her nape, then making her hypocritical, then made him extracted with a firm twisted rope as an animal is drawn from its burrow. The mastery of this wondrous art is subtle, and God is the Granter of success.

I say: As for "idhaqah," it has become customary to them as a literal usage, because it is common in afflictions, hardships, and what touches people from them. They say: "So-and-so tasted misery and harm," and "God made him taste punishment": the perception of the effect of harm and pain is likened to the perception of the taste of bitterness and nastiness. [[His phrase "what is perceived of the taste of bitterness and nastiness" is, in another's version, "the taste of bitter and nasty," and perhaps it is "al-murr al-bashi'" without the waw. (A)]] As for "libas," it was likened to it because it envelops the wearer: whatever of incidents covers a person and clings to him. As for applying "idhaqah" to the garment of hunger and fear, since it has become an expression for what covers and clings to them from these two, it is as if it were said: "He made them taste what covered them of hunger and fear." For this kind of expression there are two approaches that must be fully grasped, for the objection arises only from one who has missed them. The first:

That one looks at the borrowed-for thing (al-musta'ar lahu), as he does here. Similar is the verse of Kuthayyir:

Lavish of cloak, when he smiles laughing... the necks of wealth are pledged by his laughter. [[By Kuthayyir. Al-ghamr: abundant. He likened giving to a cloak, since it protects the honour of its owner or conceals the poverty of the petitioner, so he borrowed the cloak for it by way of explicit metaphor (tasrihiyyah), and the attribution of "ghamr" to it is tajrid, since it suits the likened thing. It may also be said that "ghamr" denotes water that submerges the stature of one immersed in it, so it is permissible that it likens giving, in that it guards its owner's honour, to the cloak, making it an explicit metaphor, and the attribution of "ghamr" to it becomes the attribution of the likened-to to the likened, in common with the generality and benefit of each. It is said: a man is "ghalaqa" when he is vexed and angry, and a pledge is "ghalaqa" when the pledgee owns it and its owner cannot redeem it, and that was their custom. The meaning: when he laughs, the wealth becomes angry, thinking it will be taken and owned by another, or it settles in the hands of the beggars and they own it. "Raqab al-mal" is a metonymy (majaz mursal), meaning its very substances.]]

The borrowing of "cloak" for kindness, because it protects the honour of its owner as a cloak protects what is thrown over it. Describing it with "ghamr," which is the attribute of kindness and bounty, not the attribute of a cloak, looks to the borrowed-for thing. The second:

That one looks at the borrowed thing itself, as in his saying:

"'Abd 'Amr contends with me over my cloak... gently, O brother of 'Amr ibn Bakr."

"To me is the half that my right hand possesses, and to you is what you may wrap yourself with of it, half." [[He borrowed "contending" for the sword's extending to him until it came between them, like a thing pulled by two people. He borrowed "cloak" for the sword, by the common factor of each keeping the other and neither being independent of it. "I'tijar" is tarshih, meaning wrapping the turban or wrapping oneself, which suits the cloak. It is possible that the whole construction is of the type of tamthil (extended metaphor). We seek refuge with God from the sudden arrival of vengeance and death in heedlessness.

The original is: "wa-libas al-khawf" (and the garment of fear). It is also read: "libas al-khawf wal-ju'" (the garment of fear and hunger).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verses 114–115:

When He admonished them with what was mentioned about the state of the town (qarya) and what it was afflicted with because of its disbelief and the evil of its deeds, He followed this, with the particle fa' in His words ﴿So eat﴾, by turning them away from the practices of the Jahiliyya (the time of ignorance before Islam) and its corrupt doctrines that they had been upon. He commanded them to eat of what Allah had provided for them, the lawful and good, and to give thanks for His bounty in that. He said: ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾, meaning: obey Him. Or [it means]: if your claim is true that you worship Allah by worshipping the idols, because they are your intercessors with Him. Then he enumerated for them the things Allah has forbidden, and forbade them from making things unlawful and lawful by their own whims and ignorance, without following what Allah had legislated through the tongue of His prophets.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 16, verses 114–115:

When He admonished them with what was mentioned about the state of the town (qarya) and what it was afflicted with because of its disbelief and the evil of its deeds, He followed this, with the particle fa' in His words ﴿So eat﴾, by turning them away from the practices of the Jahiliyya (the time of ignorance before Islam) and its corrupt doctrines that they had been upon. He commanded them to eat of what Allah had provided for them, the lawful and good, and to give thanks for His bounty in that. He said: ﴿if it is Him that you worship﴾, meaning: obey Him. Or [it means]: if your claim is true that you worship Allah by worshipping the idols, because they are your intercessors with Him. Then he enumerated for them the things Allah has forbidden, and forbade them from making things unlawful and lawful by their own whims and ignorance, without following what Allah had legislated through the tongue of His prophets.

Its accusative (naṣb) form, al-Kadhib (the lie), is governed by "wa-lā taqūlū" (and do not say), meaning: "and do not say the lie concerning what your tongues describe of the cattle as lawful and unlawful, in your saying, ﴿This is what is in the bellies of these cattle, exclusively for our males, and forbidden to our wives﴾, without that description being supported by a revelation from God or by an analogy resting upon one." The lām in it is like its lām in your saying: "and do not say, concerning what God has made lawful, that it is unlawful." And his saying, ﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful﴾, is a substitution (badal) for "al-kadhib."

It is also permissible for it to be linked to "taṣifu" (your tongues describe), with the meaning of "saying" implied, i.e.: "and do not say the lie concerning what your tongues describe, so that you say, 'This is lawful and this is unlawful.'" You may also put "al-kadhib" in the accusative as the object of "taṣifu," and make "mā" a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah), and link ﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful﴾ to "wa-lā taqūlū," meaning: "and do not say, ﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful﴾, because of the description your tongues give to the lie; that is, do not forbid or permit on account of a statement that your tongues utter and that circulates in your mouths, not on account of proof and evidence, but a mere bare assertion and empty claim."

If you ask: what is the meaning of "their tongues describing the lie"? I say: it is from eloquent and rhetorical speech; it makes their saying as though it were the very essence and pure substance of falsehood, so that when their tongues utter it, they have adorned the lie with its finery and given it its form, as in their saying: "Her face describes beauty," and "Her eye describes magic."

It has been read as "al-kadhib" in the genitive, as an attribute (ṣifah) of "mā" understood as a verbal noun, as if it were said: "for their description of the lie," meaning "of the liar," as in the Exalted's saying, ﴿with false blood﴾ (Qur'an 12:18). The intended "description" is their describing the cattle as lawful and unlawful. It has also been read as "al-kadhib" in the nominative, the plural of kadhūb, as an attribute of "al-alsinah" (the tongues), and in the accusative as an exclamation of reproach (ʿalā al-shatm). Or it may mean "the lying words," or it is the plural of kaddhāb from your saying kadhaba kadhāban; this was mentioned by Ibn Jinnī.

As for the lām in ﴿li-taftarū﴾ (that you may fabricate), it is the lām of causation that does not imply the sense of purpose. ﴿A little enjoyment﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., their benefit in what they are upon of the actions of the Jāhiliyyah is a small benefit, and its punishment is great.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on surah 16, verses 120–122:

﴿Indeed, Abraham was a community (ummah)﴾. There are two interpretations. The first is that he alone was a community among the communities. [Al-Zamakhshari said: "Regarding His words, 'a community,' there are two interpretations. The first is that he alone was a community among the communities..." Ahmad said: The second interpretation is strengthened by His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Then We revealed to you: follow the religion of Abraham, a hanif﴾ (16:123). That is, he was a community that people would follow, to acquire good things from him and to walk in his blessed footsteps. Even you, despite your high station, We have revealed to you to follow his religion and conform to his way. And God knows best.] This is because of his perfection in all the qualities of goodness, as in the verse:

*"It is not far-fetched for God
to gather the whole world into one man."*

[*"Say to Harun, the imam of guidance,
at the gathering of the crowded assembly:
you, with all your power,
are not like al-Fadl, the one man."*

*"It is not far-fetched for God
to gather the whole world into one man."*

This is by Abu Nuwas, addressing Harun al-Rashid, who was inclined to pardon al-Fadl al-Barmaki when he threatened him with death, out of jealousy after hearing of al-Fadl's extreme generosity. The *ba'* entered the predicate of *laysa* to emphasize the negation. He supported this by the verse: it is not far-fetched for God to gather all the qualities of the world into one man, like al-Fadl. This is what the wording apparently conveys, but it contradicts the requirement of the context of seeking favor. So the meaning is: do not let jealousy of al-Fadl arise in you, for his generosity is only one of your qualities, since God is able to gather all the qualities of the world in you, and He has done so. It is also reported as "from God" instead of "on God," and as "unprecedented" (*bi-mustabda'*) instead of "far-fetched" (*bi-mustankar*).]

According to Mujahid: he was a believer alone while all the people were disbelievers. The second interpretation is that *ummah* means *ma'mum*, that is, people follow him to take goodness from him, or it means one who is followed, like *rahlah* (the destination one aims for) and *nukhbah* (the chosen one), and similar words that come in the pattern *fi'lah* in the sense of *maf'ul*. This would be like His words: ﴿Indeed, I am making you an imam for the people﴾ (2:124).

Al-Sha'bi related from Farwah ibn Nawfal al-Ashja'i, from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "Indeed Mu'adh was an *ummah*, devoutly obedient to God." I said: "You are mistaken; it is only Abraham." He said: "The *ummah* is the one who teaches goodness. The *qanit* is the one obedient to God and His Messenger." [Al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* reported it through 'Ulayyah from Mansur from 'Abd al-Rahman from al-Sha'bi: "Farwah ibn Nawfal al-Ashja'i told me that Ibn Mas'ud said..." and so on. But in it there is no "You are mistaken"; rather it says: "It was said to him: indeed it is Abraham." It also says: "Mu'adh ibn Jabal used to teach people goodness, and he was obedient to God and His Messenger." Al-Hakim also reported it through Shu'bah from Firas from al-Sha'bi from Masruq from 'Abd Allah: "Indeed Mu'adh was an *ummah*, devoutly obedient to God." A man from Ashja', called Farwah ibn Nawfal, said: "That was Abraham." 'Abd Allah said: "We used to liken him to Abraham..." (the hadith). 'Abd al-Razzaq also reported it, and through al-Hakim's chain, al-Thawri related from Firas similarly.] Mu'adh was like this. It is also related from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that when he was asked, "Will you not appoint a successor?", he said: "If Abu 'Ubaydah were alive, I would appoint him; if Mu'adh were alive, I would appoint him; if Salim were alive, I would appoint him. For I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Abu 'Ubaydah is the trustworthy one of this community; Mu'adh is a devoutly obedient *ummah* to God, between him and God on the Day of Resurrection there are none but the messengers; Salim is intensely loving toward God, and if he did not fear God, he would not disobey Him.'" [I have not found it.] This is the same meaning: he was an imam in religion, because imams are teachers of goodness.

The *qanit* is one who stands by what God has commanded. The *hanif* is one who inclines toward the religion of Islam and does not turn away from it. He denied polytheism of him in refutation of the disbelievers of Quraysh, who claimed that they were upon the religion of their father Abraham. ﴿Grateful for His bounties﴾ (16:121). It is reported that he would not eat his midday meal except with a guest. One day he found no guest, so he delayed his meal. Then he saw a group of angels in the form of men. He invited them to the food, but they appeared to him as if they had leprosy (*judham*). He said: "Now it is obligatory to eat with you," thanking God that He had granted him health and tested them. ﴿He chose him﴾ (16:121): He singled him out and selected him for prophethood. ﴿And guided him to a straight path﴾ (16:121): to the religion of Islam. ﴿A good reputation﴾ (16:122). According to Qatadah: it is that God makes him remembered, so that there is no people of any religion but they claim allegiance to him. It was also said: wealth and children. And it was said: the saying of the one praying among us: "As You blessed Abraham" (*kama sallayta 'ala Ibrahim*). ﴿And indeed he is among the righteous﴾ (16:122): among the people of Paradise.
